papers.title: Runout mechanism of landslides in alluvial basins with emphasis on the impact and erosion effects
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Landslide runout is a critical factor in risk assessment, and runout distance is the most widely used indicator of mobility. Runout distance is determined both by the landslide's initial conditions and through interactions with erodible substrates, which can affect momentum by altering basal friction or by increasing overall flow volume, generally increasing runout distance. After initiation, landslide processes can be separated into two phases: an impact phase and a runout phase. While erosion during the runout phase has been considered in prior studies, impact forces themselves have been overlooked. Here, we combine fieldwork in SE Tibet, laboratory tests, and numerical modelling to resolve the dynamics and effect of impact loading on landslides in alluvial basins. Impact-loading ring-shear tests and numerical simulations, backed up by field evidence, indicate that impact forces can near-instantaneously generate high excess pore water pressure within a saturated substrate, reducing basal friction of the landslide mass and extending runout. Both impactor and substrate properties, including stiffness and compressibility, control the impact load and duration, leading to different runout patterns and landslide mobilities. We find that the farthest runout occurs at an intermediate impact level, when the normal component of peak impact stress matches the self-weighted stress of the final deposits, as this condition most effectively liquefies the substrate. The findings highlight the importance of considering substrate properties for both erosion and impact during landslide runout analyses, particularly those occurring in alluvial basins.

papers.title: Projected warming and extreme precipitation changes across the himalayan arc using WRF regional climate simulations
A methodological approach for land use planning in hill towns of India: a case of Shoghi special area of Shimla
papers.summary: Land is a finite, immovable, and valuable resource that supports diverse societal needs. Rapid population growth and consequent changes in land use have intensified development pressures, making systematic land use planning essential, particularly in India’s environmentally sensitive hilly regions. Topographical constraints, limited developable land, climatic variability, and high exposure to geohazards further complicate development planning in hill towns. However, contextual land use planning for Indian hill towns remains relatively under-researched. This study develops a systematic framework for land use planning and allocation in hill towns by integrating environmental, infrastructural, and hazard-related considerations. An integrated Analytic Hierarchy Process–Geographic Information System (AHP–GIS) framework was applied to the Shoghi Special Area, Shimla, using 20 criteria grouped into natural setting, built environment, and hazard proneness. Expert judgments were used to derive criterion weights, with all pairwise comparison matrices satisfying the consistency requirement Consistency Ratio (CR) ≤ 0.10; goal-level Consistency Ratio (CR) = 0.0%; group consensus = 96.9%. Category weights were 37.6% for hazard proneness, 33.8% for natural setting, and 28.6% for the built environment. Earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility received the highest individual weights. Criterion layers were prepared in ArcGIS 10.4.1, standardized using a five-level rating scale, and aggregated through weighted linear combination across 443 land facets delineated according to IS 14,496 (Part 2): 1998. Results indicate that 55.53% of facets scored above 50, while only 16.03% exceeded 60. No facet attained the Most Suitable or Extreme Suitability classes. The findings demonstrate that natural setting constitutes the principal constraint on development capacity, highlighting the need for context-sensitive, risk-informed, and sustainable land use planning in Indian hill towns.

Studies were further categorized into model types (empirical, physically based, machine learning, probabilistic, hydro-mechanical models).

papers.title: Urban green space research, knowledge gaps and opportunities for advancing nature-based solutions: Lessons from Bangladesh
Exploring rainfall thresholds for shallow landslides using effective half-life precipitation indices and cluster analysis: a case study in Santos and Guarujá, Brazil
authors: Victor Arroyo da Silva do Valle
papers.summary: Abstract Santos and Guarujá have a long history of shallow landslides, with rupture surfaces generally reaching depths of up to 3 m. The slopes are underlain by gneissic and migmatitic bedrocks, where failures occur in immature residual soils, often at the soil–saprolite interface and exacerbated by anthropogenic interventions. An extreme rainfall event in March 2020 triggered a major disaster, resulting in 41 fatalities. This study investigates the relationship between landslides and rainfall using simple and effective half-life rainfall indices over a 5-year period (2018–2022). Rainfall accumulated over 1, 12 and 96 h was computed using the Automatic Rainfall Half-Life Cluster System (ARHCS), while K-means clustering and threshold identification were performed. The dataset comprised 136 landslide rainfall indices in Santos, 178 in Guarujá, and 665 non-occurrence rainfall events. The results show that effective half-life rainfall indices reduce data dispersion compared with simple rainfall indices, particularly when analyzed using K-means clustering. They also identify distinct rainfall reference levels from moderate to extreme, associated with induced, occasional, multiple, and generalized landslide scenarios. The established threshold levels are consistent with the empirical curves adopted by the São Paulo Preventive Civil Defense Plan, while soil moisture data from CEMADEN stations provide additional support for interpreting the landslide-rainfall relationship. The study demonstrates that the application of the Effective Half-Life method to landslide forecasting improves the definition of rainfall conditions associated with occurrence and non-occurrence rainfall events. Validation of the results indicated better predictive performance for the Half-Life method (98%) than for the Simple method (88%).

papers.title: Landslide hazard on Kefalonia island, Greece.
Satoyama destruction and homogeneity as sources of environmental vulnerability in Tokyo
Landslides impacting road infrastructure under climate and weather influences: a systematic literature review with descriptive bibliometric insights
papers.summary: Climate change is modifying the rainfall conditions that trigger landslides, threatening road networks essential for economic development and disaster response. This systematic literature review with descriptive bibliometrics analyses 80 publications (2009–2025) from Scopus and Web of Science. Unlike previous reviews, which address landslide–climate interactions without an infrastructure focus or road-network vulnerability without a climate driver, it requires the simultaneous presence of four domains: landslide processes, road infrastructure, risk assessment, and weather or climate drivers. A standardized extraction form recorded region, scale, method, climate input, risk components and indirect impacts for every study. Output grew by 11% per year, but 45% of the studies come from Asia and 26% from Europe, whereas South America and Africa together contribute 8%. Susceptibility or hazard was assessed in 90% of the studies, but only 21% completed the hazard–consequence–risk chain. Quantitative climate projections were used in 25%, and only four studies combined them with a complete risk chain. Network connectivity was modelled in 9% and indirect losses were quantified in 10%. The methodological families are complementary: physically based models represent changing triggers but rarely exceed slope scale, data-driven models assume that present factor–landslide relationships persist, and network models quantify consequences but seldom use projections. We propose a framework linking climate projections, susceptibility/hazard, road exposure and vulnerability, network consequences and risk management, and derive recommendations for road authorities, transport agencies, disaster risk managers, and policymakers, including multi-temporal inventories with road attributes, multi-scenario network assessments and climate-sensitivity analyses in technical guidelines.

papers.title: Water Resource Changes and Natural Hazards
papers.summary: Water resources are undergoing significant transformations due to the combined influences of climate change, population growth, land‑use change, and intensified human exploitation of natural systems. These transformations increasingly contribute to the emergence and amplification of natural hazards such as floods, droughts, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF), land subsidence, landslides, and water quality degradation. Understanding the relationship between changing water resources and associated hazards is essential for developing effective risk management and sustainable water governance strategies. This chapter examines the dynamics of water resource changes through a series of global case studies representing diverse environmental and socio‑economic contexts. Key examples include glacier retreat and GLOF in the Himalayas, groundwater depletion and land subsidence in South Asia, large‑scale flooding in the Mississippi River Basin, drought and water scarcity in the Horn of Africa, and salinization in delta regions such as the Mekong Delta. Additional sections explore emerging water hazards in rapidly urbanizing regions, hydrologically triggered landslides, and water quality degradation linked to eutrophication and pollution. By synthesizing these case studies, the chapter highlights the interconnected roles of climate variability, human activities, and hydrological processes in shaping water‑related hazards. It also emphasizes the importance of integrated risk assessment, technological monitoring systems, ecosystem‑based management, and participatory governance in mitigating these risks. The findings demonstrate that sustainable water resource management must incorporate interdisciplinary knowledge, adaptive policy frameworks, and proactive hazard mitigation strategies to enhance resilience in the face of ongoing environmental change.

papers.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning Applications in Hazard Modelling and Risk Assessment
papers.source: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
papers.summary: This chapter provides a systematic assessment of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methodologies utilized to evaluate the vulnerability to numerous hazardous occurrences, including air pollution, urban heat islands, floods, and landslides. Climate change is resulting in more frequent hazardous events in densely populated metropolitan areas; it is crucial to provide cities with effective tools for risk assessment and preparedness. Resulting in a thorough methodology for hazard susceptibility modeling that encompasses data preprocessing, feature selection, model development, interpretation, and validation of susceptibility maps, along with illustrations from global and continental datasets. The chapter addresses the issues of ongoing risk assessment in safety-critical sectors, highlighting the necessity for sophisticated techniques to analyze pertinent data and successfully manage unforeseen incidents.

The Medog sub-dataset cannot be shared due to national regulatory restrictions on high-resolution remote sensing data covering border areas; it was used only as an independent cross-regional generalization test set.

papers.title: Numerical analysis of coal seam spontaneous combustion effects and preventive berm design for composite slope stability in arid open-pit mines
papers.summary: This study investigates the spontaneous combustion of shallowly buried coal seams at the toes of dump–end-wall composite slopes in open-pit mines and its implications for slope stability. An integrated approach combining theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and field investigations was employed to identify the mechanism of coal-fire initiation, assess its influence on slope stability, and develop a mechanism-informed prevention strategy. The results reveal a mechanism whereby stress redistribution, shear deformation, fracture evolution, and oxygen migration collectively govern coal-fire initiation in composite slopes. The interaction between waste-dump and end-wall slopes induces significant shear stress concentration and deformation within the slope toe, promoting fracture propagation and coalescence. Under hot and arid conditions, the resulting fracture networks provide oxygen pathways that enable spontaneous combustion of shallowly buried coal seams without direct outcrop exposure. Coal burning further reduces slope stability through coupled thermo-mechanical degradation, decreasing the factor of safety from 1.668 to 1.560. A counterweight berm strategy was developed to regulate toe stress conditions, suppress fracture connectivity, and interrupt oxygen transport pathways, increasing the factor of safety from the initial unbermed value of 1.668 to 1.758. The findings provide a geomechanical basis for the assessment and proactive prevention of coal-fire hazards in composite slope systems.

papers.title: Determination and analyses of rainfall thresholds for landslide initiation in the Greater Durban Metropolitan Region, Eastern South Africa
Prediction of shear process in granular geomaterials using acoustic emission
papers.source: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Geotechnical Engineering
papers.summary: The progressive failure of granular geotechnical materials acts as a critical precursor to landslide occurrence. To explore the feasibility of acoustic emission (AE) for early warning of such failures, direct shear tests were performed under eight shear rates to reproduce landslides with different deformation rates. AE signal analysis reveals that energy, ring down count, b-value and spectral centroid (Sc) evolve systematically throughout shearing. Specifically, the spectral centroid redshifts from 350 to 250 kHz, marking the development of macroscopic fractures. Integrating these AE signatures with shear stress evolution, the shear process is categorised into four stages: densification, elasticity, strain hardening and residual strength. Using 11 AE features, a convolutional neural network–long short-term memory hybrid deep-learning model embedded with spatial attention is constructed to automatically recognise shear stages, reaching a prediction accuracy of 94.52%. The attention module emphasises pre-failure key features and enhances model performance and interpretability. It is demonstrated that AE monitoring combined with deep learning can effectively identify precursor signals of shear failure in granular media under laboratory direct shear conditions, providing a preliminary methodological reference for the future development of landslide early warning systems.

Comment on egusphere-2026-4364
papers.summary: Abstract. Monsoon mountain landslide inventories face a trigger-attribution problem: failures caused by road construction can be credited to rainfall when the inventory is observed only quarterly or annually. In two adjacent watersheds in Darchula district, Far-Western Nepal where bulldozer roads began in 2017, we combined daily PlanetScope imagery (2017–2025), gauge and CHIRPS rainfall at each failure, daily road-construction records, and a quarterly inventory. Failures absent on the last clear image before a construction date and present on it were classed construction-coincident failure (CCF, n = 173 along about 69 km of road); failures mapped from 2016 imagery, before any road existed, gave a pre-road natural baseline (PRN, n = 127). Attribution proceeded by exclusion. The failures were not rainfall-driven: 63.6 % fell on dry days by gauge and 78.6 % by CHIRPS, with no rainfall correlation at any timescale. They tracked the construction front rather than the older road, 87.3 % lying within 50 m of the same-day front against 28.9 % of the old road, and they formed a distinct population, smaller and less elongate than the natural failures. One third never reached the inventory, and 60 % of those that did had failed on dry days, events a quarterly record would assign to the monsoon. Persistence was then modelled as a second-stage outcome: south-facing aspect and failure size were its dominant and most stable controls across penalised regression, Random Forest, and SHAP, and a four-variable pre-construction map placed about 90 % of persistent failures in terrain flagged unsuitable beforehand, holding on an independent watershed. Thus, daily imagery isolates a construction trigger that seasonal inventories conflate with rain, and yields a transferable basis for siting spoil before a road is cut.

papers.title: Initiation mechanism and movement characteristics of the catastrophic Caotan landslide triggered by the Ms 6.2 Jishishan earthquake on 18 December 2023 in Gansu, northwestern China
papers.summary: Abstract Background On 18 December 2023 (CST), an Ms 6.2 earthquake struck Jishishan County, Gansu Province, northwestern China. The catastrophic Caotan loess landslide–mudflow, located approximately 14.8 km from the epicenter, was triggered simultaneously. Because the landslide caused extensive damage, affected a large area, and resulted in substantial casualties, we conducted a detailed investigation comprising field surveys, UAV surveys, borehole drilling, trench observations, and in situ tests. We analyzed the topography, geological setting, hydrological conditions, and geometry of the landslide. Results Strong seismic shaking initiated slope failure in the source area. The displaced mass rapidly transitioned into a mudflow and traveled down the Qijia Valley, producing an unusually long runout over gentle terrain. We discuss the probable initiation mechanism, the transition process from sliding to flow, and the movement characteristics using evidence from the field investigation. Conclusions We identify the principal factors controlling the initiation and long-runout movement of the Caotan landslide. These findings provide insight for mitigating similar hazards in northwestern China and other loess-covered regions worldwide.

papers.summary: Outline : In this chapter, we illustrate the use of split bulk–tail models and subasymptotic models motivated by extreme-value theory (EVT) in the context of hazard assessment for earthquake-induced landslides. A spatial joint areal model is presented for modeling both landslide counts and landslide sizes, paying particular attention to extreme landslides, which are the most devastating ones.

papers.title: Innovations in Water Resource Monitoring for Natural Hazard Management
papers.summary: Effective monitoring of water resources is essential for managing natural hazards that are closely linked to hydrological processes, including floods, droughts, landslides, and coastal inundation. As climate change, rapid urbanization, and environmental degradation intensify the frequency and magnitude of water-related disasters, traditional monitoring systems alone are no longer sufficient to support timely hazard detection and risk mitigation. Recent technological innovations have significantly enhanced the ability to observe, analyze, and predict hydrological dynamics across multiple spatial and temporal scales. This chapter examines the evolving landscape of water resource monitoring and highlights the role of emerging technologies in strengthening natural hazard management. It discusses advancements in satellite remote sensing, soil moisture monitoring, Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and artificial intelligence-based data analytics. These technologies provide high-resolution, real-time information about environmental conditions, enabling more accurate forecasting and more effective early warning systems. The chapter also explores how integrated monitoring frameworks support proactive disaster risk reduction and adaptive water management strategies. Furthermore, institutional and governance challenges related to data sharing, infrastructure development, and capacity building are considered. The discussion emphasizes that technological innovation must be accompanied by coordinated policy frameworks and international collaboration to maximize the benefits of modern monitoring systems. By improving the accuracy, accessibility, and timeliness of hydrological information, innovative monitoring technologies play a critical role in enhancing resilience to the water-related hazards and promoting sustainable water resource management.

Enhancement of plant growth and soil stabilization by seaweed polysaccharides in the red soil region of Southern China
papers.summary: Red soil is the second most extensively eroded soil type in China, predominantly distributed in the southern regions. Vegetative measures are widely recognized as an effective approach for controlling soil erosion in red soil areas, as they enhance slope stability and substantially reduce soil loss. However, during the early growth stages, the short and fine roots of plants are unable to extend beyond the shear failure surface, which constrains their capacity to stabilize the surface soil. To address this limitation, researchers have introduced seaweed polysaccharides as a soil ameliorant. Nevertheless, the specific mechanisms by which seaweed polysaccharides influence plant growth, root-soil complex mechanics, and the erosion resistance of red soil remain poorly understood. Accordingly, an experimental study was conducted to investigate the enhancement of plant growth and soil stabilization by seaweed polysaccharides in red soil. The results indicate that (1) seaweed polysaccharides exhibited an optimal concentration range for improving red soil. At concentrations below 2%, seed germination, plant height, and stem growth were promoted, whereas concentrations exceeding 2% exerted inhibitory effects. (2) In terms of mechanical properties, seaweed polysaccharides significantly enhanced the shear strength of the soil. Compared with the control group, application of seaweed polysaccharides increased the cohesion and internal friction angle by 103.68% ~ 180.52% and 13.92% ~ 31.76%, respectively. When seaweed polysaccharides acted in conjunction with plant roots, the improvement was further amplified, with increases of 143.33% ~ 220.65% in cohesion and 14.83% ~ 39.45% in the internal friction angle. (3) Under simulated rainfall conditions, the sediment yield from the slope significantly decreased with increasing seaweed polysaccharide addition. papers.title: Finite element analysis of coupled hydro seismic effects on rock slope stability at a tunnel portal in the Lesser Himalaya
papers.summary: Abstract Rock slope stability in tectonically active mountainous regions is controlled by the combined influence of structural discontinuities, groundwater conditions, and seismic loading. This study presents a comparative finite element analysis of equivalent-continuum and combined-continuum modeling approaches to evaluate the stability of a tunnel portal slope in the Lesser Himalaya under dry, groundwater, rainfall infiltration, and pseudo-static conditions. Under dry conditions, the equivalent continuum model yields a factor of safety (FoS) of 4.3 with a maximum total displacement of 0.062 m, whereas the combined continuum model, incorporating foliation joints, predicts a lower FoS of 3.34 and a higher displacement of 0.21 m. Groundwater and rainfall infiltration further reduce the FoS in both models; in the equivalent continuum model, the FoS decreases to 3.73 and 3.60, whereas in the combined continuum model, it reduces to 2.87 and 2.62, respectively. Under combined transient rainfall and pseudo-static loading, FoS decreases significantly, reaching minimum values of 2.15 and 1.41 for the equivalent and combined models, respectively. The results demonstrate that equivalent continuum models tend to overestimate slope stability by neglecting structurally controlled failure mechanisms, whereas combined continuum models provide a more realistic representation of stress concentration and deformation localization. The findings indicate that neglecting discontinuities can lead to non-conservative stability predictions under coupled hydro-mechanical and seismic loading, particularly in Himalayan rock slopes.

papers.title: Hydrological Dynamics of Debris Flow-Prone Pyroclastic Catchments: A Budyko-Based Modeling Approach
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced geohazards in pyroclastic slopes are known to be influenced by antecedent soil wetness, but the assessment of this condition based on the catchment water balance is still unexplored. A lumped Dynamic Water Balance Model (DWBM) based on the Budyko framework is developed to characterize the hydrological behavior of eight landslide-prone catchments underlain by pyroclastic deposits over limestone bedrock in Campania, Italy. Using monthly rain-gauge, satellite, and reanalysis data between 2003 and 2023, model parameters representing catchment retention, evapotranspiration efficiency, maximum soil storage, baseflow response, and groundwater losses were calibrated against the discharge, estimated from reanalysis runoff, for seven ungauged catchments and from a stage–discharge relationship for one gauged catchment. This allowed an assessment of the consistency of reanalysis runoff for setting up hydrological models of ungauged catchments. During calibration, the models reproduced discharge satisfactorily (RMSE = 11.66–25.95 mm; NNSE = 0.80–0.90; KGE = 0.76–0.91), although the performance decreased in some catchments in model validation (RMSE = 13.60–28.97 mm; NNSE = 0.61–0.92; KGE = 0.55–0.91). Monte Carlo and Sobol analyses revealed distinct parameter sensitivities, with evapotranspiration efficiency, catchment retention, and maximum soil storage contributing directly to model output variability, while groundwater-related parameters were primarily influential through interactions with other parameters. Physically interpretable relationships of model parameters with catchment characteristics were found, allowing a hydrological characterization of poorly gauged pyroclastic catchments. Modeled soil storage provides a physically meaningful proxy for antecedent slope wetness, potentially supporting the assessment of rainfall-induced geohazards.

papers.title: Dynamics of Groundwater vs. Surface Water and Natural Hazards
papers.summary: This chapter examines the dynamic interactions between groundwater and surface water systems and their collective influence on natural hazards in a changing climate. Moving beyond the traditional hydrologic divide, it emphasizes the physical, geochemical, and geomechanical linkages that connect subsurface and surface processes across scales. The discussion begins by framing groundwater and surface water within the integrated water balance, highlighting how exchanges between streams, aquifers, soils, and the atmosphere regulate hydrologic variability. It then explores how these interactions shape hazard regimes, including floods, droughts, landslides, land subsidence, and coastal salinization. Groundwater storage is shown to modulate flood peaks through antecedent moisture conditions and bank storage, while also providing long-term buffering during droughts through hydrologic memory. Conversely, excessive groundwater extraction alters hydraulic gradients, reduces baseflow, induces land subsidence, and increases vulnerability to saltwater intrusion in coastal regions. The chapter further analyzes the role of pore-water pressure in slope instability and the geomechanical consequences of aquifer compaction, emphasizing irreversible storage loss and infrastructure risk. Coastal aquifers receive the particular attention due to the combined pressures of pumping, sea-level rise, storm surge, and density-dependent flow processes. Throughout, the chapter underscores the necessity of integrated monitoring and modeling approaches, coupling surface hydrodynamics, groundwater flow, and climate projections, to anticipate compound hazards and guide sustainable water management. Ultimately, resilient hazard mitigation requires conjunctive water governance that aligns hydrologic science with long-term environmental and socio-economic planning.

papers.title: Natural Hazard Mitigation
papers.summary: This chapter examines how Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM) can function as a comprehensive framework for natural hazard mitigation in an era of increasing climatic variability, environmental degradation, and socio-economic exposure. It argues that floods, droughts, landslides, storm surges, and water quality crises should not be understood as purely natural events, but as socio-hydrological risks shaped by land use, infrastructure design, governance quality, and the interaction between human and ecological systems. Within this perspective, IWRM offers a practical basis for reducing disaster risk by integrating water, land, ecosystems, and institutions at the basin scale. The chapter explores how IWRM contributes to mitigation through coordinated flood and drought management, watershed protection, groundwater regulation, ecosystem restoration, pollution control, and adaptive governance. Particular attention is given to the role of water quality hazards, including contamination, disease outbreaks, and chemical risk, which often intensify after floods and droughts and can produce impacts that exceed direct physical damages. The discussion also emphasizes the importance of combining structural measures such as dams, levees, and drainage systems with non-structural measures including land-use planning, early warning systems, participatory governance, and nature-based solutions. By embedding hazard mitigation within broader water governance, IWRM helps address exposure, vulnerability, and long-term resilience simultaneously. The chapter concludes that while implementation challenges remain significant, especially in fragmented institutional contexts, IWRM provides an essential foundation for risk-informed, adaptive, and equitable approaches to hazard mitigation and sustainable development.

papers.title: An intelligent thermokarst landslide detection method incorporating physics-driven multi-feature integration in cold–arid alpine regions
papers.summary: Global warming accelerates permafrost degradation in cold–arid alpine regions, resulting in frequent thermokarst landslides that pose serious threats to transport corridors and regional ecological security. In these environments, pronounced surface fragmentation, weak spectral contrast between landslide deposits and surrounding materials, and dynamic water–thermal disturbances lead to blurred boundaries and unstable feature expressions, limiting the effectiveness of single-modality optical or SAR-based detection methods. To address these challenges, this study proposes an intelligent thermokarst landslide detection method based on physics-driven multi-feature integration. Guided by the ‘water–heat–mechanics’ coupling mechanism, a multidimensional feature set integrating optical, SAR, DEM, spectral indices, and texture metrics is constructed to capture moisture-related variations, roughness contrasts, freeze–thaw disturbances, and topographic constraints. A lightweight TokenKAN-UNet is further developed by combining KANConv2D for nonlinear feature extraction, token-level global modelling, and multi-scale feature fusion, enabling precise boundary delineation with high efficiency. Experiments along the China–Pakistan Friendship Highway on the Pamir Plateau show that the proposed method achieves higher IoU, F1-score, and Recall than U-Net, U-Net++, and TransU-Net, while requiring only 15.18 M parameters and 31 ms/step inference. PDP analysis provides a descriptive interpretation of model responses in relation to the physical rationale for feature selection.

papers.title: PlanetScope Imagery for Slow-Moving Landslide Monitoring: Processing Strategies, Validation and Insight on Transient Processes
papers.summary: Abstract. Landslides can be affected by transient deformation, which can be difficult to measure, particularly for landslides in remote locations. Because these movements can be precursors to ruptures, monitoring landslides with high frequency satellite data is a key objective of research in mountain landslide hazards. The PlanetScope constellation, with a daily revisit frequency, has a demonstrated capability for tracking surface motion based on the correlation of image pairs. However, the results of the image correlations are affected by a series of artifacts coming from the acquisition geometry, acquisition timing, pair-choice strategy or type of matching algorithm. The choice of these strategies and algorithms has not been validated quantitatively by independent measurements from moving areas, and no integrated and validated workflow is yet available to process the whole chain of data. In this context, we propose an integrated, open-source, and containerized software for calculating displacement fields using PlanetScope imagery. We used several years of GNSS data from two monitored slow-moving landslides in Peru to evaluate the strategies of image pairing and correlation algorithms (block matching - BM and more global matching - MGM). We first show that commonly estimated errors on stable areas are substantially underestimating the errors on moving areas. We then show that the image acquisition timing within the day significantly impacts the results due to illumination effects. By combining these results, we show that both the BM and MGM algorithms can perform well, but the BM algorithm appears to be more effective at capturing fast-moving objects, while the MGM algorithm gives better results in low-velocity areas and reduces systematic errors. We also show the benefits of combining short-term pairs (<3 months) with long-term pairs (yearly) for a better mapping of transient movements. The strategies were applied to three Peruvian landslides and demonstrated that

papers.title: Cambio climático y resiliencia social en comunidades altoandinas: estudio en Ecuador y diálogo con Perú
papers.source: REDSA Revista Ecuatoriana de Desarrollo Social y Ambiental
papers.summary: To analyze perceived risks, adaptation, and social resilience in a rural high Andean community in Ecuador and discuss comparative questions relevant to Peru. A convergent, cross-sectional, non-experimental mixed-methods study included 64 convenience-sampled participants and eight key informants. Data came from a survey, interviews, and participatory mapping. Analyses included descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, non-parametric tests, and thematic analysis. Droughts, frosts, and landslides were the most frequently perceived hazards. Social resilience was moderate (M = 3.21; SD = 0.58), with the highest score in bonding social capital and the lowest in access to information and institutional resources. Resilience was associated with adaptive capacity (rs = .62; p < .001), and participation with strategy diversity (rs = .57; p < .001). In this case, community cohesion coexists with institutional and material gaps. The findings inform future comparisons with Peru but are not empirical evidence about Peru and cannot be generalized across countries.

papers.title: Classification and prediction
Natural Hazard Assessment
papers.summary: This chapter presents the fundamentals and practical applications of remote sensing for monitoring water resources and water‑related hazards. It reviews how electromagnetic radiation interacts with water, vegetation, soil, and urban surfaces, and how optical, microwave (including Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)), thermal, and gravimetric observations enable the mapping and quantification of hydrological variables. Key satellite and airborne data sources, including Landsat, Sentinel, Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM)/ Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM), Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP), Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE)/ GRACE‑Follow On (GRACE‑FO), and altimetry missions, are introduced with emphasis on their resolution, revisit frequency, and suitability for operational monitoring. The chapter then summarizes core analytical techniques such as spectral indices, change detection, image classification and machine learning, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation mapping, thermal retrievals, and data assimilation with hydrological models. Applications are highlighted for the flood detection and assessment under all-weather conditions, drought monitoring using vegetation, temperature, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and water storage anomalies, and landslide/sediment hazard mapping through optical change analysis, topography, and radar-based deformation monitoring. Finally, the chapter emphasizes multi-sensor integration, cloud computing platforms, and model coupling as pathways to near‑real‑time hazard intelligence and improved decision support for sustainable water management and disaster risk reduction.

papers.title: Cultured Mining Governance in the Perspective of Siyasah Dusturiyah: Evidence from Sand Mining in Boyolali Regency
papers.source: Journal of Law Politic and Humanities
papers.summary: Mining activities in Boyolali Regency provide economic benefits but also generate socio-environmental and governance challenges. This study examines sand and rock mining governance through the perspective of Siyasah Dusturiyah and proposes a governance model based on prophetic values. Using a socio-legal approach, the study analyzes mining practices in Cepogo, Musuk, and Selo District through field findings, legal analysis, and environmental data. The findings demonstrate that mining governance problems extend beyond licensing compliance. In Cepogo, mining supports local livelihoods while generating externalities affecting water, roads, air quality, noise and slope stability. In Musuk, problems involve spatial discrepancies, environmental documentation, and inadequate public participation. In Selo, hydrological risks and inadequate post-mining management indicate the ecological consequences of extraction. From the perspective of Siyasah Dusturiyah, mining authority constitute an amanah that must be directed toward maslahah and justice (‘adl), while Sadd al-Dhari’ah provides a preventive principle for avoiding foreseeable harm. Based on these findings, this study proposes Cultured Mining, an integrated governance model combining legal, ecological, participatory, economic, and prophetic cultures through preventive licensing, responsible extraction, partivipatory monitoring, and restoration-oriented post-mining evaluation. The model offers a framework for transforming mining governance from permit-centered extraction toward socially responsible and ecologically sustainable resource management.

Clustering of Ultra-Large Landslides in the Upper Yellow River Based on Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) Dating
papers.summary: Dating landslides is essential for establishing the temporal framework needed to link landslide occurrence with tectonic uplift, climate change, and river incision, and for assessing the stability of ancient landslide slopes. Although previous studies have dated landslides using a variety of methods, these methods have been constrained by difficulties in sample acquisition or limits on their effective dating range. To address these limitations, in this study, 10 ultra-large ancient landslides in the Longyangxia–Jishixia section of the upper Yellow River, which were selected based on their geological structure, stratigraphy, and lithology, were sampled at specific points for optically stimulated luminescence, using five different approaches. The reliability of each sample was tested, and the results were used to investigate the relationship between geological time, climate change, and the clustering of landslides. OSL dating is feasible for these deposits when supported by clear stratigraphic contacts, bleaching tests, and independent validation. The ultra-large landslides in the study area yield four provisional age groups (130–110, 50–30, 12–9, 5–3 ka; 95% HPD after uncertainty propagation). The primary cause of landslide clustering in each period was also determined. The clustering was primarily controlled by tectonic uplift associated with the Gonghe Movement and by climate-driven increases in rainfall and river erosion.

This condition is increasingly relevant in Aceh Province, North Sumatra, and West Sumatra, which in 2025 face various hydrometeorological disasters, such as floods, flash floods, and landslides, that have the potential to affect social conditions and regional development. This study aims to identify and group regencies/cities based on the similarity of multidimensional characteristics of education, employment, environment, welfare, and economy using the K-Means clustering method with Euclidean distance. The data used are secondary data for 2025 on 75 regencies/cities in the three provinces. The analysis stages include data standardization, determination of the number of clusters, cluster formation using the K-Means algorithm, and interpretation of group characteristics based on centroid values. The analysis results produce five clusters with member proportions of 4.00%, 34.67%, 2.67%, 26.67%, and 32.00%, respectively. Cluster 1, consisting of Medan, Deli Serdang, and Langkat, is characterized by very high education and employment, while Cluster 5 shows relatively the highest welfare and economic characteristics. These characteristic differences show that development improvement does not occur uniformly across all regions. This study investigates the interplay between groundwater and surface runoff in controlling suspended sediment dynamics within the Galabre catchment, a 20 km² Mediterranean mountainous catchment characterized by extensive badland areas. Using an End-Member Mixing Analyzing framework that accounts for event-specific variability in end-member chemistry, the study quantifies surface runoff and groundwater contributions during 86 flood events spanning three hydrological years. Hydrological analyses reveal clear seasonal contrasts in the generation of surface runoff and groundwater flow rates. Surface runoff contributions during floods vary from 0 to 50 % of the instantaneous flow rate, with higher proportions during the dry spring/summer season (May–September) and lower values in autumn/winter. Surface runoff and groundwater flow rates are strongly correlated with event rainfall accumulation, while groundwater-related variables also show sensitivity to antecedent rainfall over 15 days, highlighting their dependence on long-term hydrological connectivity. Marked seasonal differences in hydrosedimentary processes were observed. This suggests that high amounts of fine sediments are mobilized on hillslopes during these floods, leading to high suspended sediment concentrations and moderate flow rates in the river network, associated with sediment deposition. Proper design parameters and approach of SCP are essential to achieve the desired ground improvement performance. However, stability checks for slopes with SCP seem not to be straightforward due to various assumptions. How the SCP-treated ground should be modelled is still quite challenging due to the complexity of the ground behaviour from the interaction between SCP and unimproved soft clay. In this chapter, the stress concentration ratio (SCR) was extensively investigated with various modelling approaches, such as unit cell models, 2D plane strain model and full 3D model. Eco-Compatible Stabilization of Loess Mine Slopes Using a PDADMAC-Based Polymer–Mineral Composite: Hydraulic, Mechanical, and Ecological Performance
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced surface erosion of aeolian loess slopes in open-pit coal mines threatens slope stability and ecological reclamation, whereas conventional rigid protection and ordinary soil stabilizers can hardly reconcile soil reinforcement, impermeabilization, and vegetation compatibility. Here, poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) was compounded with nano-SiO2, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium bentonite, and sodium lignosulfonate into a modified PDADMAC-based composite (MPDC). An L18(37) orthogonal array optimized the mix proportion (0.80, 0.50, 0.15, 1.60, and 0.10 wt.% of dry soil for PDADMAC, nano-SiO2, CMC, bentonite, and lignosulfonate, respectively), which was evaluated by shear and permeability tests, scanning electron microscopy, a 480 min rainfall test on a 38° slope model, and six-month field monitoring. The optimum mixture raised cohesion from 18.5 to 41.8 kPa and the friction angle from 26.8° to 32.7°, and cut saturated hydraulic conductivity by 74.3%. Under 480 min of rainfall, sediment loss and erosion ratio were 142.3 g m−2 and 4.7%, i.e., 88.7% and 88.8% below untreated loess, and cumulative infiltration fell by 85.4%. After six months, the treated 0–5 cm layer retained 46.6 kPa cohesion and a 2.2% fissure ratio (versus 20.8%); after 48 h of scouring, soil loss and sliding area were only 5.3 kg m−2 and 1.5 m2 per 100 m2, with Medicago sativa survival above 91.3%. MPDC thus couples soil reinforcement, seepage control, and ecological restoration.

Waste Dump Slope Stability and Toe Berm Stabilization Under Moisture-Induced Strength Degradation of a Thick Soft Loess Foundation
papers.summary: A waste dump at a copper–molybdenum mine in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia, China, was investigated. Direct shear tests, three-dimensional finite element analysis, and field monitoring were used to investigate the effects of moisture-induced strength degradation of the loess foundation on slope stability and the effectiveness of toe berms. As water content increased from 10% to 18%, the cohesion and internal friction angle of the loess decreased by 74.1% and 15.0%, respectively. As the shear strength of the foundation decreased, deformation became increasingly concentrated near the slope toe. A continuous shear strain band developed from the toe into the loess foundation, while the factor of safety (FoS) decreased from 1.93 to 1.08. Field monitoring showed that cumulative horizontal displacement increased from the crest toward the toe, a spatial pattern qualitatively consistent with the numerical results. With the 20 and 40 m toe berms, FoS increased to 1.25 and 1.35, respectively. With the 40 m berm, the maximum absolute vertical displacement in the model and maximum shear strain decreased by 81.0% and 74.1%, respectively, compared with the case without a berm. These results help characterize the stability of waste dumps with similar thick soft loess foundations and the effects of toe berms.

Assessing soil erosion in understory-eroded forestlands based on the three-dimensional index of stratified vegetation volume
papers.source: Frontiers in Forests and Global Change
papers.summary: Introduction Traditional vegetation indicators such as fractional vegetation cover (FVC) and NDVI capture only horizontal extent and fail to distinguish the erosion–reduction functions of canopy, understory, and litter layers, often overestimating soil conservation in forests with closed canopies but degraded near‑surface vegetation. Methods We developed an empirical model to assess the soil erosion index (SEI) based on Stratified Vegetation Volume (cover × leaf area index or litter depth) across three vertical layers. SEI was measured from 17 standard runoff plots in a typical red soil erosion area of southern China and extrapolated to 46 natural forestland sites using a two‑variable empirical model based on bulk density and gravel content (cumulative grade accuracy: 91.1% within ± 1 erosion grade). Results Using extrapolated SEI as dependent variable and vegetation volumes of the three layers as independent variables, the three‑variable regression model performed best ( R 2 = 0.650, RMSE = 0.104). Regression coefficients followed a clear hierarchy: understory (−0.186) > litter (−0.046) > canopy (−0.040), indicating that understory vegetation contributed approximately 4.6 times more to erosion reduction than the canopy. The two‑indicator model (understory + litter) achieved the same grade classification accuracy (96.3%) as the three‑indicator model, offering a simplified pathway for rapid assessment when resources are limited. Discussion These results establish near‑surface vegetation as the core functional layer for forest soil conservation and provide a quantitative tool for diagnosing forest soil health and guiding restoration prioritization in degraded subtropical forests.

papers.title: Small Dolbeault eigenvalues near stability walls
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: We determine the small spectrum of the Dolbeault Laplacian on trace-free endomorphisms of Hermitian–Einstein bundles near intersections of slope-stability walls. On a compact Kähler manifold of dimension at least two, consider an extension of \(\bigoplus_{j=1}^kF_j\) by \(F_0\), where the factors are pairwise nonisomorphic and stable of equal slope at the limiting Kähler class, and every extension component is nonzero. Write \(r_i=\operatorname{rk} F_i\) and let \(\epsilon_j\) be the Einstein constant of \(F_j\) minus that of the extension. In the chamber \(\epsilon_j>0\), exactly \(k\) eigenvalues tend to zero. They agree, to relative error \(O(\sum_j\epsilon_j)\), with the eigenvalues of \(\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_k)+r_0^{-1}vv^*\), where \(v_j=\sqrt{r_j\epsilon_j}\). The estimate is uniform in all positive ratios of the slope gaps. Thus the ranks and slopes determine the leading spectrum even when the gaps vanish at arbitrarily different rates. For two factors we obtain \(\lambda_1=\delta-D\delta^2+o(\delta^2)\), where \(\delta>0\) is the quotient Einstein constant minus the subbundle Einstein constant and \(D\ge0\) is given by the Green operator of the graded connection. We also determine the first eigensection through order \(\delta\) in every spatial \(C^m\) norm. Toric tangent bundles provide examples with arbitrarily many independently varying small eigenvalues.

papers.title: COMPREHENSIVE GEOTECHNICAL ASSESSMENT FOR DESIGNING A RESERVOIR FOR COLLECTING MELTWATER IN AKMOLA REGION
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Water scarcity and increasing climate variability pose significant challenges to sustainable water supply in the steppe regions of Northern Kazakhstan. This study presents a comprehensive geotechnical assessment for the design of a meltwater reservoir in Akmola region, Kazakhstan, aimed at improving water security and adapting to climate change. A pre—selected area of 105 (52°12'2" n, 68°17'38" E) was estimated based on an analysis of terrain slopes. The physical and mechanical properties of the foundation soils were characterized by field and laboratory studies. The optimal type of dam was selected by comparative analysis of soil, rock-fill and concrete alternatives. The slope stability analysis was performed using the methods of marginal equilibrium. The results show that Site 105, characterized by gentle slopes (0-1°) and favorable soil conditions, is the most suitable location. A homogeneous soil dam with a core of soil stabilized with 10% lime provides a stability margin factor of 1.569 at an embankment height of 7 m, which meets international criteria. The results obtained provide a scientific basis for designing meltwater collection infrastructure in cold, semi-arid steppe conditions.

papers.title: Integrating surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes: A systematic review and research framework
papers.summary: Abstract. Climate warming has accelerated permafrost degradation, leading to significant challenges in water circulation and transformation. Since the early 21st century, especially during the last ten years, permafrost hydrology has garnered substantial attention, yielding a wealth of research outcomes. However, a comprehensive and systematic understanding of the permafrost hydrology remains limited. This study synthesised the current knowledge through an extensive literature review and systematic analysis, establishing a foundational framework for permafrost hydrology. The framework integrated three critical dimensions: surface hydrological processes, hydrological functions of the active layer, and the hydrological effects of permafrost changes. Subsequently, the current state, trends, and challenges in permafrost hydrology research were summarised, and a holistic overview was provided. Regarding surface hydrological processes in permafrost regions, this study examined the impacts of freeze-thaw cycles on surface runoff from multiple perspectives, including the influence of active layer thawing, slope hydrological processes, river channel dynamics, large-scale permafrost hydrology, and the hydrological consequences of thermokarst formation. For hydrological processes within the active layer, the study identified the hydrological role of the active layer, key factors influencing its hydrological behaviour, and the interactions between suprapermafrost water and soil water. Concerning the hydrological impacts of permafrost thaw, this study investigated the transformation dynamics between surface and groundwater in permafrost regions by analysing the effects of climate change through increased baseflow, groundwater recharge, and subsurface runoff. Finally, this study outlined future research directions, emphasising three key areas: the application of novel observational methods, integrated surface-subsurface investigations, and the ecological and environmental impacts

papers.title: Enhancing urban water resilience through green infrastructure in Kathmandu, Nepal
papers.summary: Rapidly growing cities in developing countries, including Kathmandu, Nepal, are struggling to handle water issues driven by both urban growth and climate change. Conventional grey infrastructure is unable to address the rising problems of flooding, polluted water, and declining groundwater recharge. This work evaluates how Green Infrastructure (GI) might help make Kathmandu Valley more sustainable and enhance ecosystem resilience through better water management. This study develops an integrated urban water resilience framework for Kathmandu Valley by combining geospatial analysis, hydrological modelling, field-based assessment of GI interventions, and stakeholder-driven policy evaluation. The interdisciplinary approach enables simultaneous examination of environmental performance, spatial vulnerability, and institutional implementation challenges associated with GI adoption in a rapidly urbanising Himalayan city. GI interventions reduced surface runoff by up to 40%, improved water quality by reducing nutrient loads (BOD, nitrate, phosphate) by over 60%, and mitigated urban heat by 3–4 °C. Spatial analysis identified priority zones for GI implementation along the Bagmati River corridor and in low-lying urban areas of Kathmandu Valley. Stakeholders expressed strong public support for GI initiatives but highlighted weak institutional coordination and limited maintenance capacity as major implementation challenges. This research helps build evidence for ecological adaptation and suggests useful steps to make Kathmandu’s infrastructure more resilient, livable, and ecologically adaptive.

Non-classical Mullins-Sekerka instability during mineralization at gas-liquid interfaces
papers.summary: Abstract Diffusion-driven morphological instability, described by Mullins–Sekerka theory, predicts amplification of interfacial perturbations and wavelength selection for idealized sharp interfaces. However, natural systems rarely satisfy these assumptions. Here, we investigate barite mineralization on the growing interface of CO $$_{2}$$ gas bubbles using 3D focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) tomography, quantitative surface analysis and reactive transport modelling. Bubble morphologies exhibit diffusion-driven instability, with dominant modes consistent with Mullins–Sekerka predictions. However, the interface violates key assumptions of the classical framework; it is porous, transport active, and evolves in pore space confinement, while crystallization proceeds via heterogenous nucleation, producing a polycrystalline interface. We show that diffusion-driven instability persists under these conditions but with modified mode selection, defining a non-classical Mullins–Sekerka regime for gas-liquid interface mineralization. Such dynamics influence pore structure evolution and transport pathways in the subsurface environment.

papers.title: Investigation of dimension reduction for Bayesian calibration of a Ti-6Al-4V crystal plasticity model
papers.summary: Numerical simulation models that accurately predict the behavior of complex materials such as the aerospace-grade Ti-6Al-4V are often highly computationally expensive and contain a large number of model parameters that must be inferred by comparing the model predictions with experimental observations. Often, such calibration is carried out using deterministic optimization procedures, but these methods do not account for physical, data, or modeling uncertainties and may produce results that cannot be meaningfully extrapolated to new operating conditions not covered by the calibration experiments. On the other hand, uncertainty-aware calibration using the Bayesian framework is more robust, but it is difficult to carry out for a large number of parameters because of the curse of dimensionality and the computational expense of evaluating the simulation model many times. With this context, the contributions of this work are twofold. First, we investigate the application of Bayesian calibration, enhanced with active subspace-based dimension reduction and surrogate modeling, to a crystal plasticity finite element model that predicts the mechanical properties of a forged Ti-6Al-4V alloy. In particular, we demonstrate how dimension reduction can enable calibration in high dimensions without the use of sophisticated sampling techniques or heuristic down-selecting of parameters. Next, we study the impact of the latent space dimension (constructed through dimension reduction) on the calibrated posteriors. Most importantly, we examine how optimal single-value estimates of the model parameters differ between deterministic calibration algorithms and Bayesian point estimates, underscoring the necessity of appropriately incorporating all physical, modeling, and approximation uncertainties to ensure robust calibration outcomes.

papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: To reveal the influence mechanism of the layout of effective impervious area (EIA) on urban stormwater processes，a refined stormwater model was constructed，and upstream and downstream sub-catchments were delineated. Taking the Shuangqiaobang runoff plot in Changzhou，Southern Jiangsu，China，as a typical study area，the impact on peak flow and runoff volume were systematically analyzed by setting different scenarios of EIA increments with different locations and scales. Results showed that the location of the EIA，infiltration capacity of the original pervious surface，and rainfall magnitude are key factors affecting the hydrological response. The spatial location effect of newly added EIA is significant，with the growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume in downstream areas being significantly higher than those in upstream areas，showing maximum difference of 18.48% and 7.70% under the moderate-infiltration scenario，respectively. Pervious areas with stronger original infiltration capacity exhibit a greater proportional increase in runoff after conversion to EIA. The growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume tend to decrease with increasing rainfall return period，exhibiting an amplification effect under low-return-period rainfall events. This study provides a scientific basis for optimizing the spatial patterns of underlying surfaces in urban settings and guiding the rational layout of stormwater facilities.

Water storage in the soil affects the vapour transpiration but also its heat storage capacity, its thermal conductivity and the energy separation between latent and sensible heat fluxes. In a real scenario, the presence of bare soil is not common as most of the time some kind of vegetation may be found on top. In order to reduce the amount of vegetation responses in addition to the soil moisture estimation longer wavelength can be used. In this study we like to explore the polarimetric and interferometric response of the BIOMASS mission, which operates in P band wavelength. Polarimetry can be used to define the scattering mechanisms and is able, when using decomposition methods to separate the ground and vegetation contribution. To perform this separation a physical model is employed and fully polarimetric data is needed in order to invert for the different involved parameters. It is worth mentioning that for extracting the ground response and the corresponding soil moisture, a significant degree of penetration into vegetation is required. For this reason, SAR soil moisture inversion has traditionally been investigated with L-band. In this study we use quad polarimetry in P band to investigate the sensitivity to bare soil and vegetated soil for soil moisture estimation [R1]. papers.summary: Abstract. Floodplains exert profound control on catchment water quality by transiently storing, transforming, and releasing solutes and particulate matter as they flow through the river corridor. These dynamic environments are shaped by periodic floods that increase hydrologic connectivity, linking shallow floodplain soils to groundwater and surface water and driving abrupt shifts in solute mobility. While floodplain inundation is often assumed to flush accumulated solutes toward groundwater and surface water, floods can arise through several different mechanisms — including overbank flow, rising groundwater levels, and rainfall- or snowmelt-induced ponding — each of which likely has a distinct impact on solute transport. Here, we combine field observations with reactive transport simulations to evaluate how distinct forms of inundation impact solute mobilization from floodplains. Results from a dye infiltration experiment reveal that precipitation-driven, top-down inundation events (such as rainfall in excess of infiltration capacity) induce preferential flow through macropores. This floodwater bypasses the soil matrix and results in minimal solute exchange. In contrast, observations from a groundwater-driven, bottom-up flood show rapid increases in solute concentrations as groundwater rose into the soil profile and dissolved evaporites within the soil matrix. To generalize beyond these field observations, we use dual permeability reactive transport simulations to test how inundation type, magnitude, and timing affect net solute exchange between the soil and underlying aquifer. Simulations show that groundwater-driven, bottom-up floods drive a net gain of solutes from the aquifer to the floodplain. Top-down floods, on the other hand, lead to solute loss from the floodplain to the aquifer, but this loss can be outweighed by summer plant water demand, which limits downward percolation of floodwater. papers.title: Hydraulic behavior and solute redistribution of saline-alkali black soil: Implications for stormwater source control
papers.summary: Study Region Daqing, northeastern China, has saline-alkali soils, strong evaporation, and shallow groundwater that constrain infiltration-based stormwater source control. Study Focus We examined hydraulic behavior and water and solute redistribution in black soil amended with 0, 0.5, and 2.0% Na 2 CO 3 . Saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K s ) was measured after 0~4 wetting-drying cycles. Soil water retention was determined by the filter paper method, and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity ( K u ) was estimated with the van Genuchten-Mualem model. A complementary column experiment applied sequential rainfall depths of 10, 20, 40, and 70 mm to track soil moisture, electrical conductivity (EC), and gravel layer water EC. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Na 2 CO 3 addition reduced initial Kₛ from 3.31 × 10 −6 m/s at 0% to 2.49 × 10 −7 and 3.02 × 10 −8 m/s at 0.5% and 2.0%. Wetting-drying caused further declines, while estimated Kᵤ remained lower in Na 2 CO 3 -amended soils over most of the modeled suction range. During sequential rainfall, the 2.0% treatment accumulated more water near the surface and responded more slowly at depth. EC decreased in the upper 20 cm but increased at 20~40 cm, while gravel layer water EC increased by only 8.9%. Low hydraulic conductivity therefore restricted vertical water transmission and promoted solute accumulation within the soil profile.

papers.title: Experimental Investigation of Pervious-Impervious Concrete Layered System for Airport Runway Drainage
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Severe operational hazards, including dynamic hydroplaning and reduced visibility is caused by the accumulation of surface water on airfield pavements, while it also places significant strain on conventional airport drainage infrastructure. This research presents an experimental investigation into the use of pervious concrete as a Sustainable Drainage System for pavements of airport. Pervious concrete creates an interconnected microporous network that facilitates rapid surface runoff infiltration by intentionally reducing and omitting the fine aggregates. As the mechanical strength of Conventional Pavement Quality concrete is higher so its application in aviation environment is traditionally limited. This study evaluates the structural and hydraulic performance of various pervious concrete mix proportion by varying water-cement ratio, aggregate sizes and aggregate to cement ratio. Laboratory tests such as compressive strength and hydraulic conductivity are conducted at 7-day and 28-day curing interval. The primary goal is to optimize the mix design to get a viable balance between drainage performance and structural load-bearing capacity to ultimately determine the feasibility of deploying pervious concrete in specific airfield zones such as runway shoulders, taxiway edges and apron margins. Building upon these structural and hydraulic assessments, the research explores the broader operational impacts of replacing traditional impermeable surfaces. By preventing water pooling, the optimized porous matrix serves as an active safety intervention, preserving friction to the pavement and drastically cutting down aquaplaning risks during heavy rainfall. Additionally, adopting this decentralized storm water related pollutants such as unburnt hydrocarbons and heavy metal runoffs before infiltrate local water tables. papers.title: Reducing the Footprint of Agriculture Through Sustainable Land Management Practices
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Soil degradation and desertification represent major challenges for Mediterranean ecosystems. Unsustainable land management practices have altered vegetation structure and density, accelerating soil erosion and desertification processes. In response, many Mediterranean regions have adopted sustainable land management strategies, reducing human pressure such as agriculture's footprint. Here we present and five cases around the Mediterranean where such strategies have been implemented instead of unsustainable ones and we highlight their outcomes. Ιn Stornara and Tara, Puglia, Italy, where aquifer irrigation and unlicensed wells are widely used, worsening groundwater depletion and salinisation. Through organic farming practices in table grape production, soil organic matter is increased, enhancing water retention. Integrating native species into the farming system increases resilience for pests and diseases. At the same time, biodiversity conservation within agricultural production is also retained as cover crops are used as well. In Tamia, Fayoum, Egypt Integrated soil fertility management, improved plant varieties, water diversion and drainage. The area is under pressure because of degraded soil and water quality. More specifically, the area of Tamia is characterised by salt-affected soils whilst also being calcareous – containing over 10% calcium carbonate. To tackle these, several strategies have been implemented including salt-tolerant species and varieties have been selected, application of organic and bio fertilizers, mulching, and subsurface drainage system. papers.title: Unsaturated Soil Behavior Under Repeated Traffic Loading in Arid Climates: A Scenario-Based Numerical Study of Road Subgrade Performance Under Assumed Climate-Analogue Suction Pathways
papers.summary: Road subgrade response in arid regions is governed by the unsaturated state of the soil, yet pavement design frameworks represent moisture mainly through empirical, largely equilibrium environmental adjustments rather than through the explicit evolution of matric suction during wetting and drying. Climate influence is represented by a two-suction concept that separates the annual-average drying trend from the critical post-rainfall wetted state. The suction pathways are not derived from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) output: their end-of-life values (140 and 55 kPa) are prescribed, and they are labelled Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 analogues only because their direction and ordering are qualitatively consistent with the projections of the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) for arid regions. They are treated throughout as assumed scenario parameters. All soil, traffic and deformation parameters are representative literature-based values; no measured retention, resilient modulus or rutting data are used, so every result is a conditional model output and not a validated prediction. Under the assumed high-emission analogue the computed year-20 subgrade rut depth is 22.0 mm (parameter-perturbation range 12-31 mm), reaching the 20 mm rut-depth threshold adopted here between years 19 and 20, against 6.5 mm for the constant-climate baseline and 11.1 mm for the moderate analogue. A one-at-a-time sensitivity screening ranks the assumed pathway shift (+15.5 mm) first, followed by design suction (+4.6/-1.8 mm), the initial-strain (ε0) scaling and the exponent β, with traffic growth least influential.

papers.title: Multivariate analysis of compound hydroclimatic extremes in snow-fed sub-catchments: an application for climate-resilient water management of Narayani Basin, Nepal
papers.summary: Compound hydroclimatic extremes challenge water management worldwide due to their complex and nonlinear hydrological impacts. Drought-to-flood (DtF) events occur when prolonged dry periods are followed by rapid wet anomalies with distinct impacts from regular floods. Such events occur across diverse hydroclimatic settings; in heterogeneous snow-fed basins, DtF behaviour is governed by precipitation variability, antecedent soil-moisture conditions, snow processes, and, where present, reservoir regulation. This study investigates DtF transitions across six sub-catchments of the Narayani River Basin, Nepal, using monthly precipitation (17 stations), streamflow (6 gauges), remote sensing soil moisture, and historical drought–flood records. Historical DtF events were fitted with monthly Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) signals, and sensitivity analysis of three ΔSPI thresholds (1.0, 1.25, and 1.5) identified 1.25 as the optimal criterion for distinguishing meaningful DtF transitions. The calibrated ΔSPI framework identifies DtF events and integrates ΔSPI–ΔSSI regression with multivariate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of ΔSPI, ΔSSI, and ΔSWDI to investigate coupled hydroclimatic controls and process-level DtF dynamics. Results reveal pronounced spatial contrasts across hydroclimatic regimes. Highly snow-dominated Budhi Gandaki exhibits weak or opposing ΔSPI–ΔSSI responses during snow storage, followed by strengthened rainfall–runoff coupling during snowmelt (R2 up to 0.96). Moderately snow-influenced sub- catchments display mixed rainfall–runoff responses (R2 = 0.02–0.79), reflecting varying contributions of snowmelt and rainfall, whereas rainfed reservoir- regulated Tadi Khola and Rapti show weak pre-monsoon responses during reservoir filling (R2 = 0.001–0.96) and shift to strong monsoon coupling (R2 = 0.75–1.00) during reservoir release. PCA shows that PC1 explains 40%–100% of the joint ΔSPI–ΔSSI–ΔSWDI variance, with contrasting loading directions between pre

papers.title: Scalable and locally mass-conservative simulation of basin-scale variably saturated groundwater flow
papers.summary: Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km^2, contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. By contrast, a vertically lumped coarse-space preconditioner takes the full three-month step on every mesh, requiring four to ten linear iterations per Newton step and reducing wall-clock time by a f

papers.title: FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems. 1. Theory and applications with intercode benchmarking
papers.summary: Abstract FLOWS (FLOws of Water and Solutes in soils) is a dynamic physically-based model to simulate water flow and solute transport in the soil–plant–atmosphere system. The numerical code was written in MATLAB. One-dimensional vertical transient water flow is simulated by numerically solving the 1D form of the Richards equation (RE) using an implicit, backward, finite differences scheme with explicit linearization. As for the solutes, the code solves the 1D Advection Dispersion equation (ADE) by an explicit, central difference scheme, allowing for a relatively easy inclusion of non-linear adsorption and other non-linear processes. The model produces information on the time evolution of (among many other outputs): soil water contents and pressure potentials in the soil profile; solute (tracers, adsorbed, volatile and reactive solutes) concentrations in the soil profile; water and solute uptake and actual evapotranspiration for simulated crops; deep percolation water and solute fluxes; root uptake of water and solutes, also in presence of water and osmotic stresses; water fluxes and related solute fluxes to runoff; drainage water fluxes and related solute fluxes; irrigation fluxes computed by the model; and temperature in the soil profile. Compared to other existing models, some specificities of FLOWS model are: (1) integrated simulation of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus transformations and transport contextually to the simulation of water contents and fluxes; (2) macroscopic root uptake; (3) irrigation management, by allowing to optimize the time scheduling and volumes according to some criterion based on the average pressure head in the root zone; (4) the possibility of running multi-site simulations, which may be especially important for spatially distributed simulations; and (5) an interactive graphical user interface, allowing the user to easily handle even large input files and seeing the simulation results by graphical display of the main output variables.
