papers.title: Rainfall partitioning and contrasting local understory runoff and soil loss responses among three vegetation communities in a karst restoration area
papers.summary: Study region Puding County, southwestern China, a karst area characterized by severe rocky desertification and long-term ecological restoration. Study focus Vegetation restoration alters canopy structure and rainfall redistribution, but how these changes relate to localized understory runoff and soil loss remains unclear. We monitored 31 rainfall events in three vegetation communities dominated by Platycladus orientalis , Platycarya strobilacea , and Viburnum dilatatum . Community-scale throughfall, stemflow, and canopy interception were quantified, while runoff and soil loss were monitored in subcanopy and stem-base microplots. Mixed-effects models were used to assess rainfall, microsite, and environmental associations. New hydrological insights for the region Throughfall was the largest rainfall-partitioning component and was highest in P. orientalis (86.21%), although this community did not show the strongest erosion response. P. strobilacea had the greatest runoff and soil loss, with mean soil loss of 28.97 and 61.79 g m⁻² in subcanopy and stem-base microsites, respectively. Gross rainfall showed strong nonlinear associations with runoff and soil loss. Slope and bare-soil cover were positively associated with both responses, whereas saturated hydraulic conductivity was negatively associated. After accounting for gross rainfall, community-level throughfall fraction provided no significant additional explanatory information for subcanopy runoff or soil loss. Because stemflow to individual stem-base microplots was not directly measured, stem-base responses were interpreted as integrated microsite responses.

papers.title: Evaluating multi-benefit strip-cropping systems for climate-resilient agricultural landscapes in Malawi
papers.source: CGSPace A Repository of Agricultural Research Outputs (Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research)
papers.summary: Soil erosion, land degradation, and declining soil fertility continue to threaten agricultural productivity and food security across Malawi, particularly in sloping landscapes where runoff and soil loss are prevalent. These challenges are expected to intensify under climate change due to increasing rainfall variability and more frequent extreme weather events. While various soil and water conservation technologies have been promoted, their adoption by smallholder farmers has often been constrained by labor requirements, land-use trade-offs, and limited short-term economic benefits. Consequently, there is growing interest in integrated farming approaches that simultaneously enhance productivity, improve resilience, and conserve natural resources. This study evaluated the performance of strip-cropping systems as a strategy for developing resilient agricultural landscapes in Malawi. The approach integrates contour-aligned grass strips with maize and legumes within productive farmland to reduce runoff and erosion while maintaining crop production and generating livestock feed. The study aimed to assess the agronomic, fodder, and conservation potential of alternative strip-cropping configurations across contrasting slope conditions and to identify systems capable of balancing productivity and sustainability objectives. Field experiments were established on farmer-managed fields representing gentle (5–15%) and steep (15–25%) slope categories. Four cropping systems were evaluated using a randomized complete block design with three replications per farm: (i) Grass–Maize–Grass (GMG), (ii) Grass–Maize–Grass–Maize–Grass (GMGMG), (iii) Grass–Maize–Legume–Maize–Grass (GMLMG), and (iv) a maize monocrop control. Mixed-effects models were used to assess treatment effects while accounting for farmer-to-farmer variability. Results showed that cropping system significantly influenced maize grain yield and overall system productivity, whereas slope category and treatment × slope intera

papers.title: Bridging nature-based solutions, smart technologies, and traditional wisdom for sustainable water management: a multi-decadal evaluation of bamboo-based systems in degraded ravine landscapes
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are increasingly recognized as sustainable approaches for addressing water insecurity, land degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate resilience. However, robust long-term field evidence quantifying their hydrological and ecological effectiveness remains limited. This study presents a multi-decadal (1985–2025) evidence synthesis evaluating bamboo-based NbS for restoring degraded ravine landscapes in India by integrating long-term field observations, experimental watershed investigations, hydrological monitoring, project datasets, and peer-reviewed literature. Results demonstrate that bamboo functions as living hydrological infrastructure by enhancing rainfall retention, increasing infiltration, reducing runoff and sediment transport, improving soil quality, and accelerating ecological recovery. Bamboo-based interventions reduced runoff by 80–90%, soil loss by 85–95%, and sediment yield by over 90%, while stabilizing gullies within 2–3 years. Infiltration increased substantially (up to ∼140 cm h−1) together with improvements in soil organic carbon and micro-ecological conditions. Economically, bamboo systems generated annual returns of ₹33,500–48,000 ha−1 with internal rates of return of 18–22%. The study proposes an integrated Nature-Based Hydrological Engineering framework, establishing bamboo as a scalable, climate-resilient solution for watershed restoration, erosion control, and sustainable water management in degraded landscapes worldwide.

papers.title: Stable water isotopes as critical constraints for ecohydrological flux partitioning in a West African basin
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the added value of stable water isotopes in constraining ecohydrological flux partitioning within the Bétérou basin, a 10,000 km² tropical savanna watershed in northern Benin. It leverages a unique five-year record of high-frequency isotope measurements in river water at the outlet and in precipitation. Using the tracer-enabled, distributed model EcH2O-iso, we evaluated how different calibration datasets influence the representation of internal flux partitioning, in particular runoff generation from surface and subsurface pathways, in a region where evapotranspiration (ET) dominates the water budget. A multi-objective calibration was performed across four scenarios, ranging from a baseline using only outlet discharge to a comprehensive setup incorporating intra-basin discharge and isotopic tracers. Our results demonstrate that isotopic tracers are essential for realistically reproducing internal flow partitioning. The inclusion of isotopes drove the model to mobilise older groundwater reservoirs, leading to increased simulated water ages and the dampening of stream isotopic signals. Scenarios calibrated solely on outlet discharge showed high fit for the hydrograph but simulated minimal subsurface contribution, contrary to field evidence from instrumented catchments. Isotopes provided only indirect constraints on ET, whose influence on water partitioning was governed primarily by root water uptake as modulated by land cover. These findings suggest that monitoring strategies in tropical environments where data are often scarce and monitoring priorities must be carefully weighed, should consider the inclusion of isotopic tracers alongside traditional hydrometric observations, as these constrain models to reproduce hydrological functioning for the right reasons and thus provide a more reliable basis for assessing water resources and climate change vulnerability.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of hydrological impacts of adjustable weirs in an open ditch: an experiment-modeling study on a shallow groundwater environment
papers.summary: Abstract. Adjustable weirs have been used to block ditch waters especially during wet seasons to retain more shallow groundwater in agricultural fields and forests. However, to fully verify the effectiveness of weirs, quantifying the weirs’ hydrological benefits to vegetation and nearby surface waters is important. Our study quantified the hydrological impacts of these weirs on the water balance across seasons under wet and dry years. We performed field experiments in a 2% sloped parcel with a single ditch and two weirs in Merelbeke-Melle, Belgium. Then, we used a 3D subsurface flow model (HYDRUS 5) to represent the phreatic and vadose zones underlying the regional hillslope. They were calibrated using water table levels monitored across the parcel in 2022–2026, covering both wet and dry years. Afterwards, we simulated separate scenarios for empty and full ditches under shallow and deep rooting depth parameterizations. The observed water tables show little responses with opening and closing of weirs. Meanwhile, simulations involving weir management exhibited higher water tables especially closer to the ditch due to reduced field drainage that retain more water during wet periods and also infiltration of ditch waters during dry periods. Yet this boosted water availability was partitioned mainly to runoff, storage, and excess (added) field drainage downstream of the weirs. The stream downslope (Gondebeek stream) had only little additional baseflows. Moreover, the vegetation experienced both wet and drought stresses that inhibited uptake of water gained from water management. Thus, hydrological models on weir management should properly consider the presence and sources of infiltrating ditch waters, vegetation dynamics in the field, and the meteorological context (seasonality, interannual variability).

papers.title: Field measurement of hydraulic conductivity in a compacted filtered iron ore tailings stack using mini-infiltrometer tests
papers.summary: This paper presents a field-based assessment of near-surface hydraulic conductivity in a compacted filtered iron ore tailings stack using mini-infiltrometer tests. A total of 115 in situ measurements were performed on the compacted surface, providing a dataset for evaluating the variability of near-surface field measurements under controlled suction conditions. The mini-infiltrometer results are interpreted as hydraulic conductivity values associated with the pressure head applied at the porous disk–tailings interface, not necessarily as fully saturated hydraulic conductivity. The measured values ranged from 1.14 × 10−7 m/s to 4.59 × 10−6 m/s, with an arithmetic mean of 1.31 × 10−6 m/s, a median of 1.20 × 10−6 m/s, and a geometric mean of 1.12 × 10−6 m/s. Although the results were concentrated around 10−6 m/s, the coefficient of variation was approximately 56.9%, indicating relevant relative variability. Most values were located between 5.0 × 10−7 m/s and 3.0 × 10−6 m/s, supporting the use of the geometric mean as a representative central estimate for engineering analyses. The influence of imposed suction (h0 ) was also examined; however, no systematic dependence on the applied values was identified. Comparison with published data shows that the results fall within the range reported for compacted and filtered tailings, while reinforcing that hydraulic conductivity cannot be inferred from void ratio alone. The study highlights the importance of direct field measurements for supporting seepage analyses, transient flow modelling, water balance assessments, and hydraulic characterization of filtered tailings stacks.

papers.title: Integrating Mean Weight Diameter and Environmental Sensitivity Index for Modeling Soil Erosion Risk and Land Degradation in Soils under Different Agricultural Land Uses
papers.source: The Eurasia Proceedings of Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics
papers.summary: The study area is located between latitudes (36°42′24.52″ N – 36°24′38.40″ N) and longitudes (43°38′14.98″ E – 43°22′14.58″ E), covering an area 1245 km². The elevation ranges from 283 to 1015 m above sea level. The climate classified as a transitional zone between semi-arid and Mediterranean climates. Twenty-five sites were selected within the study area. Approximately 2 kg of soil was collected per site, with samples carefully selected to ensure homogeneity. The samples were then transported to the laboratory, air-dried, gently crushed using a wooden hammer, and sieved through a 2 mm mesh sieve. Subsequently, they were stored in plastic containers for further physical and chemical analyses. Laboratory analyses included the determination of soil organic matter, calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) content, and particle size distribution, and Environmental Sensitivity Index equations were applied.The results indicated that the dominant soil textures in the study area ranged from clay to clay loam.. This variability is primarily attributed to differences in soil organic matter content and calcium carbonate levels, which reached maximum values of 2.28% and 37.2%, respectively. Furthermore, the results revealed relatively uniform sorting values across most sites, indicating a generally homogeneous particle size distribution, except for site, which exhibited a high sorting value of 2.420, reflecting poorer sediment uniformity. The study demonstrates that both water and wind erosion processes in the region are controlled by a complex interaction of natural and anthropogenic factors acting simultaneously, which significantly influence soil stability and susceptibility to detachment and transport.

papers.title: Land cover change and groundwater recharge at Jeju Global Education City
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Jeju Island relies heavily on groundwater recharged through its permeable volcanic terrain. This study examines how development of the Jeju Global Education City, where site construction began in 2009, changed surface infiltration and what this implies for groundwater recharge. Land-cover maps from 2007 and 2025 were compared over 378.9 ha of mapped cover within the legal planning boundary. Single-ring infiltration tests were carried out on Gotjawal, rough grass and artificial grass, with five trials per surface; one rough-grass trial did not finish within 300 s and was excluded from rate statistics. Under a scenario that treats artificial grass as non-recharging, the share of the site treated as sealed rose from 2.5% to 27.8%, an increase of approximately 95.9 ha. Every Gotjawal trial infiltrated faster than every grass trial, although the apparatus supports only a relative comparison. Applying published recharge fractions of 9 to 48% to rainfall on the newly sealed area gives a potential recharge loss of 102,000 to 545,000 m³ per year from sealing alone. These are conditional estimates rather than a measured change in aquifer recharge.

Biodegradable mulch films affecting surface runoff, soil erosion, and film fragment loss from farmland
papers.summary: The use of conventional plastic mulch films is a common agricultural practice that can lead to persistent plastic film fragments entering soil systems. To prevent the accumulation of these fragments, soil-biodegradable mulch films are marketed as alternatives. Unlike conventional plastic mulch, soil-biodegradable mulch films are ploughed into the soil after use, where they biodegrade over time. This study aims to elucidate the effects of soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments—following six months of application on the soil surface—ploughed into soil on surface runoff, soil erosion, and lateral mulch film fragment loss during simulated rainfall events. Our results showed a significant increase in runoff coefficient for the pre-wetted (wet run) simulations in soils with soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments compared to soils without them, while differences in sediment delivery were insignificant. In the delivered sediments, large mulch film fragments (> 2 mm) were depleted, whereas small fragments (< 2 mm) were transported approximately proportionally to the topsoil of the plots. Overall, our results indicate that film fragments can affect surface runoff on arable land, and generally, soil erosion is a pathway of soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments transport into adjacent ecosystems, which is especially effective in the case of small film fragments (< 2 mm) available from topsoil.

(1994) and Ma et al. (2022), and the cross-check on the Nipigon GeoStudio database (Abdullah et al. 2025, CC BY 4.0); all result tables and figures. papers.title: Cover crop management influences soil properties and grapevine performance across three growing seasons in a subtropical vineyard
papers.summary: Cover crop management can modify soil conditions and grapevine performance, but these responses may depend on the vegetation-management strategy and growing season. This study evaluated the effects of different cover crop management systems on soil, physiological, yield, and fruit technological variables of Vitis vinifera L. cv. Viognier cultivated in Campo Largo, Paraná, Brazil, for three growing seasons (2023–2026; 2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26). The treatments were: T1, spontaneous vegetation (white clover in winter and Cynodon spp in summer) with herbicide application in the vine row; T2, spontaneous vegetation without herbicide; T3, black oat in winter and predominantly white clover + angola grass in summer; T4, common vetch in winter and mombaça grass in summer; and T5, multispecies cover crop mixtures in winter (black oat + rye + vetch + forage radish) and summer ( Cynodon ssp + buckwheat + mombaça grass). Cover crop biomass and macronutrient accumulation, soil chemical and physical properties, soil water content, and grapevine nutritional, physiological, vegetative, yield, and technological variables were evaluated. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models accounting for repeated measurements across growing seasons, complemented by multivariate analyses. T4 (vetch and mombaça) and T5 (oats + rye + vetch + forage radish; and Cynodon ssp + buckwheat + mombaça) generally showed greater biomass production and accumulation of N, P, K, Ca, and Mg than systems based on spontaneous vegetation. Vegetation management also affected selected surface-soil properties, particularly available P, total organic carbon, total N, cation exchange capacity, bulk density, and soil water content, although responses varied among growing seasons. Grapevine leaf area (LA) and the Yield/LA ratio did not differ among treatments, whereas physiological responses were treatment- and season-dependent. The clearest yield response occurred in 2025/26, when T2 and T4 reached 11.06

papers.title: Spatial Variability of Soil Properties and Implications for Climate-Smart Rice Production in four Agricultural Zones in Anambra State, Nigeria
papers.source: Scholarly Journal of Science and Technology Research and Development
papers.summary: Spatial variability in soil properties strongly influences water dynamics, nutrient availability, and crop productivity in tropical agroecosystems, thereby affecting the sustainability of climate-smart rice production systems. This study evaluated the spatial variability of selected soil physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties across four agro-ecological zones (Awka, Anambra, Aguata, and Onitsha) of Anambra State, southeastern Nigeria. Surface soil samples (0–30 cm) were collected from georeferenced locations differing in elevation and landscape characteristics. Laboratory analyses were conducted to determine particle size distribution, bulk density (BD), saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), soil pH, and organic matter (OM). Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), correlation analysis, and principal component analysis (PCA) were employed to evaluate variability and relationships among soil properties. Results revealed considerable spatial heterogeneity across the study area. Sand content ranged from 332 to 582 g kg⁻¹, while clay content varied between 218 and 354 g kg⁻¹. Bulk density ranged from 1.346 to 1.458 g cm⁻³, whereas Ksat varied from 0.0182 to 0.0468 cm hr⁻¹. Soil pH was moderately acidic (5.3–5.7), while OM content ranged from 2.2 to 3.3%. ANOVA indicated no significant zonal differences in Ksat and BD, suggesting that micro-scale variability exerted a stronger influence than agro-ecological classification. PCA explained 96.5% of total variability, with soil texture and hydraulic properties constituting the dominant controlling factors. The findings highlight the importance of site-specific soil and water management strategies for improving rice productivity, enhancing water-use efficiency, and strengthening climate resilience in southeastern Nigeria.

papers.title: ASSESSMENT OF THE INTRINSIC VULNERABILITY OF GROUNDWATER TO POLLUTION IN THE ANGOVIA MINING AREA (CENTRAL-WESTERN CÔTE D’IVOIRE): THE PAPRI APPROACH AND HYDROCHEMICAL VALIDATION
papers.summary: Gold mining can place significant pressure on groundwater resources, particularly in fractured bedrock aquifers characterised by high hydrodynamic heterogeneity. This study aims to assess the chemical quality and intrinsic vulnerability of the groundwater in the Angovia mining area, in central-western Côte d’Ivoire. Physico-chemical and chemical analyses were carried out on the groundwater to characterise the distribution of several elements associated with mining activities, notably copper (Cu), cadmium (Cd), cyanide (CN⁻), arsenic (As), lead (Pb) and mercury (Hg). The data were analysed using statistical methods, notably Wilk’s alpha test and ANOVA. Intrinsic vulnerability was assessed using the PaPRI approach, based on the criteria of Protection, Reservoir and Infiltration. The results show spatial variability in the chemical quality of groundwater. Cu, Cd, CN⁻ and As generally exhibit low concentrations and low spatial variability, whilst Pb and Hg show significant variations between sampling points. The vulnerability assessment indicates that 80 per cent of the area is highly vulnerable and 10 per cent is extremely vulnerable, meaning that 90 per cent of the area is characterised as being highly or extremely vulnerable. This situation reflects the aquifer’s significant susceptibility to potential contaminant transfer from the surface. The combination of hydrochemical data and PaPRI mapping therefore provides a useful tool for identifying priority monitoring areas and contributing to the sustainable protection of groundwater resources in the Angovia mining area.

papers.title: WATER-ABSORBING ROADS AS SUSTAINABLE URBAN DRAINAGE INFRASTRUCTURE
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Water-Absorbing Roads as Sustainable Urban Drainage Infrastructure This project focuses on the concept of water-absorbing roads, technically known as permeable pavement systems. These roads are designed to allow rainwater to pass through a porous surface or permeable joints into the underlying layers, where it is temporarily stored in an aggregate reservoir before infiltrating into the soil or being discharged through an underdrain. The project explores different types of permeable pavements, including porous asphalt, pervious concrete, and permeable interlocking concrete pavement. It explains the functions of pavement layers, water infiltration, drainage arrangements, construction materials, and maintenance requirements. The main objective of this project is to study how permeable pavement systems can help reduce surface runoff, minimise waterlogging, and support sustainable stormwater management, particularly in urban areas experiencing heavy monsoon rainfall. The project also examines the limitations of these systems, including clogging, soil permeability, groundwater conditions, and traffic loads. This is a conceptual, literature-supported study that highlights the importance of proper site investigation, engineering design, and regular maintenance. It presents permeable roads as a potential supplement to conventional drainage systems for developing more sustainable and resilient road infrastructure.

papers.title: Application of Organic Superabsorbent Cellulosic Polymers ( OSCPs ) and Cyanobacteria on Reduction of Aeolian Losses
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Establishing biocrusts on sandy surfaces in harsh desert environments presents significant challenges due to extreme ecological conditions. To address these challenges, this study examined the effects of two organic superabsorbent cellulosic polymers (OSCPs)—carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and guar gum (GUA)—on the establishment of cyanobacterial crusts on aeolian sands, specifically using a consortium of Nostoc sp. and Microcoleus vaginatus . The optimal concentrations of GUA and CMC for maximum cyanobacterial growth were determined through preliminary optimization assays. The resulting suspensions, combining OSCPs and cyanobacteria, were applied to sandy substrates. After 60 days of inoculation, the cyanobacterial crusts were analyzed for exopolysaccharide (EPS) accumulation, chlorophyll a content, physical and chemical properties, shear strength, and compressive strength. Additionally, wind tunnel tests were conducted to measure aeolian mass flux under the different treatments. Results indicated that the cyanobacteria + CMC treatment outperformed all others, increasing chlorophyll a by 114% and EPS production by 108% to 280% depending on the EPS fraction. This treatment also enhanced organic carbon and nitrogen accumulation, crust thickness (~21 mm), shear strength (51.39 kPa), and available water capacity (+110%). Furthermore, it raised the wind erosion threshold velocity from 11.5 to 19.7 m s −1 , reducing aeolian mass flux by over 98% at wind speeds up to 19.7 m s −1 . In contrast, GUA alone resulted in the lowest compressive strength and mass flux rates. These findings suggest that combining cyanobacteria with OSCPs, particularly CMC, is an effective strategy for promoting biocrust formation and mitigating soil erosion in arid environments.

Long-Term Seepage and Stability of Tropical Railway Cut Slopes Using Satellite Hydroclimatic Data
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides threaten tropical railway infrastructure, where sparse monitoring limits the characterization of rainfall–instability relationships. This study investigated the long-term hydraulic response and stability of railway cut slopes in residual soils along a strategic railway in the Brazilian Amazon using alternative climate datasets. Satellite-derived precipitation (CHIRPS), satellite-informed soil moisture (SMAP), and gridded meteorological variables (BR-DWGD) were integrated with laboratory hydraulic relationships and field groundwater observations to define atmospheric forcing and initial hydraulic conditions. Daily sequential seepage–stability simulations spanning more than 40 yrs were performed for four representative slope inclinations. Increasing inclination reduced stability, and only the 40° slope exhibited simulated instability. Mean annual precipitation was highest during La Niña, intermediate during neutral conditions, and lowest during El Niño, whereas mean annual minimum factor of safety (FoS) followed the reverse ordering across all inclinations. Statistically significant differences supported an association between El Niño–Southern Oscillation variability and simulated stability. Mean monthly minimum FoS was lowest in April for steeper slopes, consistent with cumulative wet-season infiltration and broadly aligned with reported March–April slope-instability events along the railway. A criterion combining 7-, 15-, and 90-day rainfall accumulations provided a preliminary model-derived reference for investigating simulated instability. The underlying mechanisms involved matric suction dissipation and localized groundwater rise near the toe, without requiring full saturation of the overlying soil. Hydraulic contrasts can guide instrumentation placement. The framework supports slope screening for railway asset management and preliminary assessment of stabilization measures, providing a basis for subsequent site-specific inves

Performance evaluation of laser diffraction and sieve-pipette techniques for grid-scale hydraulic characterization of lateritic vadose zones
papers.summary: The vadose zone plays a vital role in sustaining society and ecosystems on the Earth. The complexity of vadose zones, coupled with expensive and laborious field investigations pose a formidable challenge in their characterization, and hence they are neglected in hydrogeologic studies. This study demonstrates a novel scientific framework for the grid-scale hydraulic characterization of vadose zones using the laser diffraction (LD) technique and grain-size analysis (GSA) models. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, a total of 126 vadose zone samples and 95 core samples were collected from four layers across 33 grids in a lateritic terrain of Eastern India. Thereafter, the efficacy of the advanced LD technique and the conventional sieve-pipette analysis (SP) was compared by generating grain-size distribution curves (GSDCs) and estimating vadose-zone hydraulic conductivity (K vz ) by using selected GSA models at four different depths (0–50 cm, 50–100 cm, 100–150 cm, and 150–200 cm), followed by an uncertainty analysis. Finally, the estimates of K vz based on the SP-GSA and LD-GSA models were verified using field-measured K vz . The analysis of GSDCs for different depths revealed that the LD technique yields smoother S-shaped GSDCs than the SP technique. Consistently, low uncertainty was found in the K vz estimated by the LD-GSA models (0.0002–1.203 m/day) compared to the K vz estimated by the SP-GSA models (0.0008–2.171 m/day). The verification results based on statistical and graphical indicators revealed that the K vz yielded by most of the LD-GSA models for all layers of the vadose zone are in close agreement with the measured K vz values [MAE: 0.38 to 0.89 m/day and RMSE: 0.6 to 0.98 m/day]. On the other hand, the performance of SP-GSA models was also found to be reasonable, yielding K vz values with MAE and RMSE ranging from 0.36 to 1.45 m/day and 0.64–1.74 m/day, respectively, across all the vadose-zone layers. It is concluded that the LD technique provides mo

papers.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation on microplastic and nanoplastic removal from stormwater runoff in bioretention systems
papers.summary: Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging contaminants in stormwater runoff, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Bioretention systems offer promising nature-based stormwater treatment, yet their performance remains highly variable. Biochar, particularly post-processed biochar, has demonstrated strong potential for contaminant removal; however, its effects on MNP removal, leachate quality, and plant performance in green infrastructure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the combined effects of untreated and thermal air-oxidated (hereinafter: treated) biochars and native vegetation ( Rudbeckia hirta ) on the removal of polystyrene MNPs (0.02, 0.2, and 1 μm) from synthetic stormwater runoff, leachate quality and plant performance in bioretention systems. Both biochars effectively removed nanoplastics during the early MNP-spiked storm events. Vegetation substantially reduced MNP leaching during subsequent simulated rainfall events, supported by the detection of microplastics within root tissues, indicating plant uptake. Vegetation also reduced nutrient leaching, with larger plants exhibiting more pronounced effects, highlighting the importance of enhancing plant growth for contaminant removal. Although treated biochar reduced total organic carbon leaching during initial spiking events, both biochars increased P, K, and S leaching. Overall, our findings demonstrate synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation in enhancing contaminant retention in bioretention systems, advancing green infrastructure design and sustainable stormwater management.

papers.title: Modern monsoonal recharge connects shallow groundwater to older, deeper hyperalkaline circulation in the Santa Elena Ophiolite of Costa Rica
papers.summary: Serpentinization can generate molecular hydrogen (H 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ), yet the hydrologic timescales over which fluids circulate through actively serpentinizing systems within the Critical Zone (CZ) remain poorly constrained. We investigated groundwater-surface-water connectivity and groundwater age distributions in the Santa Elena Ophiolite (SEO), Costa Rica, where strongly monsoonal recharge provides a natural setting for resolving fluid circulation through ultramafic terrain. Groundwater, surface water, and hyperalkaline springs were characterized using tritium ( 3 H), stable water isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H), discharge, infiltration, and wet/dry stream surveys. Tritium ranged from 0.06 to 0.85 TU, compared with a 2015-2022 Costa Rican precipitation mean of 1.17 ± 0.20 TU. Surface waters contained 0.53-0.85 TU, consistent with an apparent age of ~8 years, whereas hyperalkaline springs under baseflow conditions contained only 0.06-0.09 TU, indicating apparent groundwater ages >60 years. Modern recharge fractions indicate that hyperalkaline seepages comprise 0 to 9% modern water, while SEO shallow groundwater and surface waters contain 85 to 100% modern water. Bayesian mixing model results showed that SEO surface waters were dominated by recent precipitation (54%), with a smaller contribution from groundwater (24%) and hyperalkaline fluids (22%). Stable water isotopes further reveal connectivity among precipitation, shallow groundwater, and deeper hyperalkaline circulation. These results identify two coupled flow systems: young, shallow groundwater sustaining intermittent streams and older, deeper groundwater circulation feeding hyperalkaline (pH >10.8) springs. Moderate stream alkalinity (pH 8-9) and substantial streambed degassing further suggest diffuse deep-groundwater inputs across SEO’s CZ. These findings demonstrate that tropical serpentinizing systems can retain decades-old fluids while remaining hydrologically connected to modern recharge, providing

papers.title: Integrating land resource inventory and hydrology to transform rainfed agriculture towards sustainable intensification
papers.summary: Context Rainfed agriculture in semi-arid regions is constrained not only by rainfall scarcity but also by inefficient conversion of rainfall into plant-available water. Large yield gaps persist because of poor rainfall partitioning, limited soil-moisture storage, and weak integration of land, water, and cropping-system management. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated Land Resource Inventory (LRI)–hydrology framework for improving water availability and guiding sustainable cropping-system intensification in semi-arid rainfed systems. Methods The framework was developed using long-term experimental evidence from ICRISAT's heritage watersheds in Alfisols and Vertisols, integrating soil–water characterization, rainfall–runoff relationships, landform management, and water budgeting. It was subsequently applied in Bundelkhand, central India, across a ~ 5000-ha geographical landscape (~3000 ha agricultural land), using LRI-based planning, hydrological analysis, and targeted natural resource management interventions. Results and conclusions Heritage watershed results demonstrated strong contrasts in soil–water dynamics, with Vertisols (150–200 mm plant-available water) providing greater moisture-buffering capacity than Alfisols (80–120 mm). Raised-bed landform interventions reduced runoff by ~20–40% and improved rainfall retention and soil-moisture availability. At landscape scale, targeted interventions created ~731,000 m 3 of additional water-storage capacity and substantially improved shallow groundwater availability. The landscape-equivalent supplemental irrigation requirement increased from ~35 to ~78 mm as cropping systems intensified; the incremental demand (~43 mm) was comparable to the estimated additional annual runoff-harvesting opportunity (~40–45 mm), complemented by in-situ moisture conservation. papers.title: Application of the Natural Resources Conservation Service Technical Release 55 Method in Stormwater Management for Land Development Projects: A Practitioner Case Study
papers.summary: The Natural Resources Conservation Service Technical Release 55 (TR-55) method remains one of the most widely used tools for estimating runoff on small land development sites in the United States, and in many Pennsylvania municipalities it is effectively the default method required for stormwater submissions. Most published work on the method concerns its theoretical basis, particularly the curve number and the initial abstraction ratio, while comparatively little describes how practicing engineers actually apply it and defend it in review. This paper documents that practice from the perspective of a civil engineer preparing site design and stormwater management plans for land development projects in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. It describes when the runoff calculation takes place in a typical project, how the principal inputs are selected (curve number from mapped hydrologic soil groups, time of concentration from segmented flow paths with a 100-foot sheet-flow limit, and rainfall depths from NOAA Atlas 14 checked against municipal ordinances), and how pre-development conditions are established on previously disturbed sites. These choices are then illustrated through one example from current practice: a townhouse development of approximately 3.5 acres, where the calculations led to two infiltration basins and a vegetated swale. The example shows how the hydrologic result meets the ordinance requirement, while site geometry, groundwater, infiltration rates, easements, utilities, and cost determine the final facility design. Review experience shows that stormwater submissions typically require two to three cycles, and that the most frequent comments concern time of concentration, curve number documentation, and the correspondence of drainage areas with the grading plan. Illustrative computations show why these inputs attract scrutiny: on small sites, modest changes in sheet-flow length, slope, or curve number shift peak discharge noticeably. The paper argues that many

papers.title: Morphometric analysis and prioritization of Virupapura micro-watersheds using GIS and remote sensing techniques in Cauvery River Basin, India
papers.summary: Abstract Morphometric analysis is important for understanding watershed behaviour and supporting sustainable resource management, especially under changing climate and water stress conditions. This study evaluates morphometric characteristics and prioritizes eight micro-watersheds in the Virupapura sub-watershed, Cauvery River Basin, Karnataka, using GIS and remote sensing techniques. Watershed delineation, drainage extraction and parameter calculations were carried out using a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) in ArcGIS 10.8, and stream ordering was performed using the Arthur Strahler [66] method. The watershed is a fifth-order basin with a well-developed drainage network consisting of 119 first-order streams and a high bifurcation ratio (7.75–9.50), indicating structural control. Moderate drainage density (2.164 km/km 2 ) and stream frequency (2.74) suggest balanced runoff and infiltration, while the elongated basin shape and gentle slope reduce erosion risk. Hypsometric analysis showed integral values ranging from 0.151 to 0.484, indicating that the micro-watersheds are in mature to old geomorphic stages with varying levels of erosion susceptibility. Based on prioritization ranking using compound factor (Cf) values, Dholenahalli (Rank 1; Cf = 3.1) was identified as the most critical micro-watershed requiring immediate conservation measures, followed by Chikkamaskallu (Rank 2; Cf = 3.6) and K.G. Mallappanahalli (Rank 3; Cf = 3.9). These results are consistent with recent studies in semi-arid regions reporting increasing watershed degradation under climate variability and anthropogenic pressure. Given present challenges such as groundwater depletion, irregular rainfall and land degradation, the study highlights the need for targeted soil and water conservation measures, rainwater harvesting structures and scientific watershed planning for long-term sustainability.

papers.title: Impact of spatial soil variability on landslide susceptibility using 3D probabilistic slope stability analysis
papers.source: Georisk Assessment and Management of Risk for Engineered Systems and Geohazards
papers.summary: Spatial variability in geotechnical and hydrogeological parameters can substantially affect landslide susceptibility assessments. In practice, the parameters defining spatial variability, including variability level and spatial correlation length, are commonly selected from the literature because site-specific data are often limited. Such assumptions may lead to unconservative or overly conservative estimates of slope safety. This study investigates the influence of spatial variability parameters on landslide susceptibility using the Three-Dimensional Probabilistic Landslide Susceptibility (3DPLS) model. A parametric study was conducted for a simplified 2 m-thick slope considering varying levels of variability, spatial correlation lengths, sliding-surface dimensions, and problem-domain extents. Monte Carlo simulations were performed to evaluate the effects of spatial variability on the computed factor of safety and probability of failure. The results demonstrate that spatial variability substantially influences probabilistic landslide susceptibility predictions and that this influence depends strongly on sliding-surface dimensions and problem-domain extent. A worst-case spatial correlation length associated with minimum computed safety levels was identified and found to be strongly related to the sliding-surface length in the direction of movement. Furthermore, application to the 2011 Kvam landslides in Norway demonstrated that assumptions regarding spatial variability can significantly influence both the magnitude and spatial distribution of predicted landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: Analisis Multi-Kriteria Wilayah Potensi Air Tanah Menggunakan Analytical Hierarchy Proccess (AHP) dan GIS di Kabupaten Timor Tengah Utara
papers.summary: Groundwater availability is a critical issue in North Central Timor (TTU) Regency, a semi-arid region characterized by seasonal rainfall and limited surface water resources. This study aimed to map groundwater potential using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Four main parameters were analyzed, namely hydrogeology, rainfall, topography, and land cover. The AHP method was applied to determine the weight of each parameter, while GIS was used for spatial analysis and thematic map overlay. The weighting results indicate that hydrogeology is the most influential parameter with a weight of 55%, followed by rainfall (25%), topography (12%), and land cover (8%). The spatial analysis produced five groundwater potential classes: very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. Areas with high to very high groundwater potential are mainly distributed in the southern part of TTU, including Noemuti, Noemuti Timur, Bikomi Selatan, Miomaffo Barat, Insana, sebagian Mutis, dan Biboki Anleu, which are supported by productive aquifers and favorable infiltration conditions. The study demonstrates that the integration of AHP and GIS is effective as a decision-support tool for groundwater exploration and sustainable water resource management in semi-arid regions.

papers.title: Effect of printing layer thickness and sintering time on the densification, microstructure and mechanical properties of binder-jetted Ti-6Al-4V alloy
papers.summary: This study examines how printing layer thickness and sintering time jointly affect the densification, microstructure, and tensile behavior of binder-jetted Ti-6Al-4V under a fixed jetting strategy. Specimens were printed with layer thicknesses of 40, 80, and 120 μm and sintered at 1300 °C for 1–5 h. Reducing the layer thickness increased green density and refined the initial pore structure, thereby accelerating pore closure during early sintering. The 40 μm specimens reached the best condition after 2 h, with 94.4% relative density, 4.4% porosity, and an ultimate tensile strength approaches the wrought benchmark. Larger layer thicknesses required longer holding times but showed lower maximum densities within the investigated process window. Prolonged holding also promoted grain growth and possible pore coarsening, which limited further improvement. These results indicate that improving the green-body state by reducing layer thickness is more effective than simply extending sintering time, although ductility and residual defect control remain important for further optimization.

Does water resource taxation improve firm productivity and regional ecological performance? Evidence from China
papers.summary: Introduction Water scarcity is increasingly constraining global sustainable development, making it a critical policy challenge to improve economic performance while strengthening resource conservation. Methods Using the 2018 expansion of China’s Water Resource Tax Pilot Policy (WRTP) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study applies a difference-in-differences approach to firm-level and county-level data from 2012 to 2022. Results The results show that the WRTP significantly improves the total factor productivity of water-intensive firms, particularly in cities with stronger industrial foundations, the Yangtze River Economic Belt, regions with relatively abundant water resources, and larger listed firms. Environmental performance disclosure strengthens this productivity effect. Green innovation and pollution treatment disclosure exhibit significant positive moderating effects, whereas environmental supervision disclosure does not exhibit a significant moderating effect. County-level evidence further shows that the WRTP reduces water consumption intensity and the area affected by soil erosion while increasing sewage treatment capacity and investment in wastewater treatment. Discussion Overall, water resource taxation improves firm productivity while enhancing regional ecological performance, providing policy insights for advancing sustainable water governance in resource-constrained economies.

Characterization of subsurface groundwater pathways from treated wastewater effluent infiltration along the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
papers.summary: Abstract Recharge of treated wastewater to the environment is increasingly becoming a component of water resources management, especially in water-limited areas such as the Grand Canyon. Treated wastewater from the Grand Canyon South Rim Wastewater Treatment Plant has been discharged to a dry wash located along the surface expression of a fault for decades, but the fate of the wastewater is unclear. Previous research suggested possible connections between the treated wastewater discharge sites and springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon, particularly Monument spring. Additional investigations presented in this report add further evidence to the connection between the wastewater and Monument spring, utilizing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, artificial sweeteners, and stable isotopes of water. A dye trace established the first direct connection between wastewater and Monument spring where the dye added to treated wastewater took about 4–6 months to move through the subsurface and was detectable for 5 months. The persistence of wastewater tracers over time and the timing of dye movement suggests a fast subsurface flow pathway. On the basis of geologic observations of faults and jointing, groundwater flow follows a possible combination of karst and other structural pathways. The dye and wastewater tracers were monitored at other springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon and the combination of repeated dye detections and multiple wastewater tracers were only found at Monument spring. Multiple lines of evidence provide a robust tracer suite to support evidence of structural/karst controls on preferential flowpaths; faults alone are unlikely to explain the flow pathway.

Trigger–Cause Cross-Attention (TCA)
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Trigger–Cause Cross-Attention (TCA) is a deep learning framework for regional debris-flow early warning. It separately represents antecedent hydrometeorological conditions and catchment susceptibility (Cause) and short-term rainfall forcing (Trigger). Cross-attention uses the integrated Cause representation as the Query and the Trigger sequence as the Key and Value, allowing the model to evaluate rainfall forcing conditional on the catchment state. This software release provides a PyTorch implementation of TCA, including masked-reconstruction pretraining, supervised multi-task training, prediction, and a minimal input–output example with real samples. Debris-flow occurrence is the primary prediction task, supported by auxiliary magnitude regression. Exported representations and attention weights support analysis of state-dependent triggering and the temporal relevance of rainfall.

papers.title: UAV LiDAR-based identification method for valley-type debris flows in southeastern Tibet
papers.source: International Conference on Advances in Energy and Environmental Engineering (AEEE)
papers.summary: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau is characterized by deeply incised alpine valleys, steep terrain, and dense vegetation with strong spatial heterogeneity. These landscape conditions can hinder the identification of valley-type debris-flow deposits from optical imagery, especially when older fans are partly obscured by forest or when their spectral differences from the surrounding ground surface have weakened over time. To address this limitation, the Duoxiongla Valley was selected as the study area, and high-resolution topographic information was acquired using UAV-based LiDAR. Hillshade maps generated from the LiDAR-derived terrain data were used to assist the detailed interpretation of debris-flow fan morphology. The analysis primarily targeted fan deposits concealed by vegetation. Interpretation was based on fan- or tongue-shaped landforms near gully outlets, together with subtle topographic variations that remained detectable beneath the forest canopy. Optical imagery was used as supplementary evidence to check upstream channel connectivity, erosional traces, and exposed coarse materials such as gravels and boulders. The results indicate that UAV LiDAR can reveal the microtopographic form of debris-flow fans that are difficult to distinguish in optical imagery, especially in forested valley sections. A total of 48 historical debris-flow fans were identified in the study area, including 32 on the southern slope and 16 on the northern slope of the Duoxiongla River. This pattern suggests a clear aspect-related asymmetry in the distribution of debris-flow fans. The results provide useful basic data for valley-type debris-flow investigation and hazard inventory construction in southeastern Tibet.

Acid‐activated water hyacinth ( Eichhornia crassipes ) from the Nile River for textile wastewater reclamation: A comparative evaluation of anionic and cationic dye adsorption
papers.summary: Abstract Water hyacinth ( Eichhornia crassipes ) is an extremely invasive aquatic plant with notable environmental and socioeconomic impacts; however, its unique physicochemical properties offer potential for wastewater treatment through adsorption. This study investigates the acid activation of water hyacinth using acetic, sulphuric, hydrochloric, and nitric acids to enhance its performance as an adsorbent for dye removal. The aquatic plant was harvested from the Nile River, processed, and activated with each acid, and a comparative evaluation was performed. Adsorption efficiency was assessed using Methylene Blue (cationic) and Ponceau S (anionic) dyes, with removal percentage determined by spectrophotometric analysis before and after treatment. Sulphuric acid activation produced the highest adsorption capacity, achieving 94.5% removal for Ponceau S and 98.7% for Methylene Blue, attributed to improved surface area and pore structure. Response surface methodology was applied to model the effects of adsorbent dosage, contact time, and dye concentration while maximising adsorption capacity. The adsorption data were fitted to the Langmuir, Freundlich, and Dubinin–Radushkevich isotherms, and adsorption kinetics were evaluated. Sulfonated water hyacinth showed strong conformity with the Langmuir isotherm ( R 2 = 0.99, q m = 4.275 mg g −1 ) and the Dubinin–Radushkevich model ( R 2 = 0.844, Q D = 5.09 mg g −1 ), indicating monolayer adsorption and reliable model fit. Kinetic modelling followed the pseudo‐second‐order model, suggesting that chemisorption was the dominant mechanism. Overall, the study demonstrates the high potential of water hyacinth‐derived adsorbents as sustainable materials for wastewater treatment.

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-3226
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris flows often occur as intermittent surges in succession; a single event may comprise tens to hundreds of separate surges. While previous studies have focused primarily on isolated surge dynamics, the temporal evolution and statistical properties of the surge sequences as an entirety remain poorly understood. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of global debris flow datasets, including velocity, discharge, sediment volume, and inter-surge intervals. We quantitatively characterize the surge sequences by the statistic features of the key parameters, revealing 1) a general decay trend in fluctuating discharge, 2) universal distributions for flow velocity (Weibull), discharge/sediment volume (exponentially-modified power-law), and inter-surge intervals (exponential), and 3) self-similar structure in sequence organization. These findings motivate the development of a novel stochastic modeling framework that conceptualizes surge sequences through three key components: 1) The cascading thinning of mass sequences originating from Poisson processes of source failures and inter-processes of bank and bed erosions driven by hydrologic process, 2) a selection coefficient generated through Gaussian process to integrate the effective contributions of mass from multi-sources, 3) model parameter calibration using local monitoring data and experimental validation. Numerical simulations demonstrate the model's ability to accurately replicate observed surge sequences. Notably, the framework spontaneously generates a unified distribution of discharge and sediment volume in the form of a truncated power-law with an exponential cutoff. This provides a novel magnitude–frequency relationship for mass movements and can also be applied to large-scale sediment transport studies.

papers.summary: # Dataset and Python Code Description **Associated manuscript:** Quantifying Topographic Change and Sediment Export After a Debris-Flow Event Using Multi-Temporal LiDAR DEMs **Authors:** Takahide Matsuura and Yoshihiro Sato **Affiliation:** Terra Labo Inc., Japan ## 1. Overview This dataset contains LiDAR-derived topographic data, a manually digitized valley centerline, and Python scripts used to analyze topographic changes associated with a debris-flow event triggered by Typhoon Hagibis on 12 October 2019 in Minamisoma City, Fukushima Prefecture, Japan. The study compares pre-event elevation data derived from airborne LiDAR observations acquired between December 2006 and January 2007 with post-event UAV-LiDAR observations conducted on 26 October 2019, 14 days after the disaster. Digital elevation models (DEMs) with a spatial resolution of 1 m were used to quantify erosion, deposition, and sediment redistribution through DEM of Difference (DoD) analysis. The dataset consists of 11 files, including three topographic data files, one manually digitized valley centerline file, and seven Python scripts. These files are provided to document the analytical procedures and facilitate the reproducibility and verification of the results presented in the associated manuscript. ## 2. papers.title: PyDebrisFlow2D: A 2D Conservative Python Multiphysics Solver for Variable-Density Debris Flows with Voellmy Resistance, Bed Exchange, and Grain Size Segregation
papers.summary: Reliable debris-flow modelling requires the coupled treatment of rapid free-surface propagation, variable mixture composition, wet–dry fronts, basal resistance, bed exchange, and grain size segregation. This work presents PyDebrisFlow2D, a depth-averaged Python (3.13.14) solver based on seven conservative variables describing mobile fluid, layered fine and coarse solids, and two horizontal mixture momentum components. Mixture density and composition-dependent Voellmy resistance are derived consistently from the transported constituent volumes, while conservative source operators account for erosion, entrainment, class-resolved deposition, and segregation opposed by diffusive remixing. The governing equations are solved using a Cartesian finite volume method with hydrostatic reconstruction, Harten–Lax–van Leer–Contact (HLLC) fluxes, optional Monotonic Upstream-Centered Scheme for Conservation Laws (MUSCL) reconstruction, and first- or second-order time integration. Local Harten–Lax–van Leer (HLL) fallback, stage repetition, positivity repair, and adaptive time-step rejection provide additional robustness near wet–dry interfaces and strong gradients. Controlled verification experiments confirmed flux consistency, well-balanced behaviour, constituent conservation, and stable convergence for different slope limiters. The verification programme also examines the reduced segregation formulation, an alternative concentration-aware resistance closure, and the applicability limits of the depth-averaged model through targeted real-topography analyses. Across the Ritter refinement experiment, the nominal second-order scheme required 1.91–3.13× the first-order (O1) wall time while reducing the depth error; at the finest grid, the relative L1 error was 13.35× smaller for a 2.309× runtime increase. papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-5979
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. The Terrain Modification Algorithm (TMA), developed in this work, updates the computational grid at each time step, allowing topographic changes to feed back directly into the governing equations and simulated flow dynamics. The model is evaluated through three applications: validation against large-scale US Geological Survey (USGS) flume experiments, testing in an idealized parabolic geometry, and application to the 2015 debris-flow event in the La Mesilla catchment in northern Chile. The solver reproduces the measured evolution of flow thickness in the USGS flume experiments with good agreement. The idealized application demonstrates that terrain evolution is not a passive output but an active control on run-out, velocity, flow depth, and volume redistribution. The La Mesilla case further shows that coupled terrain modification promotes surge self-generation, self-channelization, and channel-plug formation, which are absent or weakened when the TMA is disabled. These results indicate that coupled terrain evolution can modify flow confinement, stress distribution, and preferential routing throughout the simulation. faDebrisFOAM therefore provides an open-source framework for investigating morphodynamic feedbacks in debris-flow propagation.

papers.title: The EMS Swiss LithoClast® Trilogy for the treatment of large bladder stones: a prospective international multicenter study
papers.summary: The best treatment for large bladder stones remains debated. The options range from open cystolithotomy to minimally invasive endoscopic techniques, including the Mauermayer stone punch and high-power laser cystolitholapaxy, and more recently the EMS Swiss LithoClast ® Trilogy, which combines ultrasonic and ballistic energy with continuous suction in a single probe and is well established in percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). We report the first prospective international multicenter experience of the Trilogy system for the transurethral treatment of large bladder stones. Consecutive patients undergoing cystolitholapaxy with the Trilogy system were enrolled prospectively at five recruiting centers in five countries between August 2023 and December 2024. Procedures were performed transurethrally through rigid sheaths of 20.8 to 26 Fr. The primary outcome was lithotripsy efficiency (preoperative CT-derived stone volume divided by probe activation time). Secondary outcomes were the stone-free rate, device safety and reliability, intraoperative urothelial trauma, postoperative complications, and surgeon-rated ergonomics and efficiency. Outcomes are reported both by intention to treat, in which patients converted to laser are counted as failures, and per protocol, restricted to procedures completed with the Trilogy system alone. Forty-four patients were enrolled (median age 76 years, range 27 to 88). Forty-three procedures were attempted; one could not proceed because of a urethral stricture. The stone could not be fragmented in two patients (4.7%), both dense calculi (1591 HU and 1280 HU), and both were converted to high-power laser, leaving 41 procedures completed with the Trilogy system alone (35 male, 85.4%). By intention to treat, the stone-free rate was 93.0% (40 of 43 attempted procedures) and 90.9% (40 of 44 patients enrolled); the per-protocol rate was 97.6% (40 of 41). papers.title: Optimization of biodiesel production from palm fatty acid distillate (PFAD) and synthesized Bambara nutshell catalyst using response surface methodology (RSM)
papers.summary: This study investigated the optimization of biodiesel yield (BDY) from palm fatty acid distillate (PFAD) using a synthesized Bambara nutshell catalyst (BNC) through a single-step esterification process and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) based on a Central Composite Design (CCD). The effects of methanol-to-oil molar ratio (8:1–12:1), catalyst loading (1–5 wt.%), and reaction time (1–4 h) on BDY were evaluated. The synthesized BNC was comprehensively characterized using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area and pore structure analyses, as well as total acid density (TAD) determination to establish the relationship between catalyst properties and biodiesel recovery. FTIR analysis revealed the presence of hydroxyl, oxygenated, aromatic, and metal-associated functional groups that support catalytic activity, whereas SEM micrographs showed a rough and porous morphology favorable for reactant diffusion. BET analysis indicated a relatively high surface area of 459.60 m 2 /g, due to the abundant accessible catalytic sites present. RSM results demonstrated that methanol-to-oil ratio, catalyst loading, and reaction time exerted positive effects on BDY, where the optimum values occurred at approximately 12:1 methanol-to-oil ratio, 5.0 wt.% catalyst loading and 4 h reaction time. Optimum predicted BDY obtained is 93.08% close to the experimental value of 94.65% (Run 14). Model adequacy evaluation through Box–Cox transformation assessment, residual diagnostics, normal probability plots, and predicted-versus-actual comparisons confirmed the robustness of the developed quadratic model. The low residual magnitude, conformity to normality, absence of outliers, and close agreement between actual and predicted yields provide strong evidence that the model was statistically adequate for BDY prediction and optimization. SHEAR RESPONSE OF UNSATURATED CLAY–GEOTEXTILE INTERFACE UNDER A WIDE RANGE OF SUCTIONS
papers.source: Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (University of Maryland College Park)
papers.summary: Soil–geotextile interface behavior governs the performance of many geotechnical systems, including mechanically stabilized earth walls, reinforced slopes, pavements, embankments, and landfill cover systems. Although the behavior of these interfaces has been widely investigated under saturated conditions, their response under unsaturated conditions remains insufficiently understood, particularly at medium- to high-suction levels encountered in compacted fine-grained soils. Most previous studies have been limited to low matric suctions (<100–300 kPa), leaving a gap in understanding interface behavior under higher suction conditions representative of many field environments.This research investigates the shear behavior of unsaturated low-plasticity clay–geotextile interfaces over a suction range of 1 to 8 MPa using two low-plasticity clay soils and two polypropylene geotextiles (woven and nonwoven). The experimental program included soil-water retention curve (SWRC) testing using the osmotic method, suction measurements using the filter paper method, and direct shear testing conducted under normal stresses of 50, 100, and 200 kPa. The study evaluates the influence of suction, normal stress, soil type, and geotextile type on the peak and post-peak interface shear behavior. The experimental results show that interface shear strength increases with increasing suction; however, the relationship is nonlinear and cannot be adequately represented by conventional linear extensions of the Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion. The increase in shear strength is primarily attributed to suction-induced adhesion, while the interface friction angle remains nearly constant throughout the investigated suction range. Nonwoven geotextiles consistently mobilized greater suction-dependent interface resistance than woven geotextiles because of their greater contact area and enhanced soil–fiber interaction. Python Scripting for PLAXIS
papers.summary: Python Scripting for PLAXIS is a comprehensive guide to developing Python-based workflows for automating PLAXIS analyses, enabling increased productivity, reduced errors and more efficient use of engineering effort in geotechnical modeling. PLAXIS is a widely used finite element software for analyzing safety, stability, deformation, consolidation and groundwater flow problems in geotechnical engineering. It is routinely applied to complex projects such as foundations, dams, embankments, ground improvement, and both surface and underground excavations. While most users rely on the graphical user interface (GUI), PLAXIS also provides powerful scripting capabilities through its command-line interface and Python API. This book demonstrates how these capabilities can be leveraged to automate repetitive modeling and analysis tasks, streamline workflows and enhance consistency in model definition and execution. Written for researchers, academics and practicing engineers alike, the book is ideal for both new and experienced PLAXIS users seeking to integrate scripting into their daily workflows and unlock the full potential of the software.

Effects of sequential hydration on water retention and shrinkage of cement-stabilized unsaturated soil
papers.summary: Early-age shrinkage cracking often compromises the durability of infrastructures constructed with cement–stabilized soils (CSS). This study evaluates a sequential hydration (SH) strategy designed to curb shrinkage while sustaining hydraulic response (e.g., degree of saturation) and mechanical performance pertinent to seepage control and serviceability limit-state design. Three hydration paths were examined: OH-100, one-time hydration at 100 % OMC; SH-80 and SH-60, compaction at 80 % and 60 % OMC respectively, followed by second-stage wetting. Soil-water retention curves (SWRCs) were measured under zero-stress and vertical stress using a stress-controllable pressure-plate apparatus and drying–wetting shrinkage was tracked over three cycles for a CSS. The results show that SH significantly reduces early-age free shrinkage while modifying water-retention behavior, hysteresis, and stress-dependent hydraulic response. Among the investigated treatments, SH at 80 % OMC produced the most favorable balance between shrinkage mitigation and hydraulic performance. SEM/EDX analyses suggest that staged hydration promotes pore-throat refinement and changes hydration-product distribution, particularly A-S-H formation. These findings indicate that SH may serve as a construction-stage strategy for reducing shrinkage cracking in cement-treated pavement bases while maintaining adequate hydraulic performance.

papers.title: Evidence for temporal decoupling of olivine weathering and inorganic carbon removal in unsaturated soil columns
papers.summary: Introduction Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a nature-based carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal technology that speeds the natural weathering process of rocks by applying finely ground silicate rocks over the land surface. It has been proposed that ERW can remove between 0.5 and 2 Gt CO 2 year −1 when deployed at scale. To investigate how soil porewater responds to the dissolution of silicate dust during enhanced rock weathering, we conducted unsaturated soil column experiments amended with olivine (Mg 2 SiO 4 ). Methods Since the main principle of ERW-based carbon removal is the reaction of atmospheric CO 2 dissolved in rainwater with silicate rocks, leading to release of base cations and bicarbonate ions, we measured cations, anions, pH, alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the leached effluent. Complementary solid-phase soil measurements of exchangeable cations, pH, total inorganic carbon (TIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) were performed to improve understanding of weathering product transport and retention, while aqueous speciation calculations provided saturation state information of relevant secondary mineral phases. Results We demonstrate that measurable olivine weathering can occur without proportional short-term export of bicarbonate or DIC, and estimates of potential CO 2 removal based on weathering-derived cation release exceeded realized inorganic CO 2 removal quantified from bicarbonate and DIC export. Furthermore, the observed increase in DOC export and decrease in surface-soil organic carbon suggest that enhanced weathering may alter soil organic carbon dynamics. Discussion The discrepancy between weathering-derived cation release and inorganic carbon export is consistent with temporal decoupling between weathering and realized carbon removal, likely caused by retention of weathering-derived products within the soil. Temperature-dependent swelling and compressibility behavior of microfiber-reinforced bentonite
papers.summary: Abstract Bentonite is widely used as a buffer material in deep geological repositories because its low hydraulic conductivity and swelling pressure help limit advective radionuclide transport. Elevated temperature, however, can cause drying and shrinkage, which may alter swelling behavior and reduce mechanical integrity. Fiber reinforcement has been proposed to mitigate these effects, but the behavior of fiber-reinforced bentonite at elevated temperature remains poorly understood. This study investigates the swelling pressure, compressibility, and consolidation behavior of glass microfiber-reinforced Na-bentonite at 22 °C and 50 °C with fiber contents of 0, 1, and 3 wt%. The fiber sensitivity of swelling pressure decreased by 42% over the 28 K temperature increase, from − 72.9 kPa/wt% at 22 °C to − 42.5 kPa/wt% at 50 °C, even though the overall swelling pressure increased with temperature. To interpret the results, a thermo-Barcelona Basic Model (BBM) framework with a volumetric homogenization fiber composite term was calibrated against the experimental data. The analysis indicates that the reduced fiber sensitivity at elevated temperature is mainly related to a decrease in the apparent fiber–matrix interfacial bond strength, τ b , from 16 to 9 kPa, whereas the bentonite-phase parameters λ(0) and p 0 changed only slightly. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of fiber reinforcement depends not only on fiber properties, but also on the thermal stability of the fiber–clay interface under hydrothermal conditions. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations showed fiber–clay contact and clay coating on fiber surfaces, supporting the proposed interfacial mechanism. Overall, the results suggest that interfacial bond stability should be considered when selecting inorganic fiber reinforcement for engineered barrier materials subjected to coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical conditions.

papers.title: Generalized Effective Stress Equation for Variably Saturated Frozen Soil
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract A unified effective stress equation for variably saturated frozen soil is proposed, theoretically verified, and experimentally evaluated. Cryostress, capillary suction stress, and adsorptive suction stress coexist when variably saturated soil is subject to freezing and thawing. Cryostress consists of three physically distinct forces at three interfaces: ice–ice bonding, ice–liquid capillary force, and ice–particle adsorptive force. Cryostress is a characteristic function of temperature and water content quantified by the cryostress characteristic curve. A generalized effective stress can be established by applying the principles of mechanical equilibrium and soil water potential equilibrium on the soil–water–ice–air representative element volume. A closed-form equation is developed where effective stress is equal to the total stress minus suction stress and cryostress. The generalized effective stress equation can be reduced to Bishop’s form of effective stress in saturated frozen soil when ice–particle adsorptive stress is neglected, to Lu and Likos’ suction stress-based effective stress in unfrozen unsaturated soil, and to Terzaghi’s effective stress in unfrozen saturated soil. The closed-form equation is experimentally evaluated using published shear strength test results for sandy soil, lean clay, and silty clay. The fitted parameters also show good consistency with independently measured soil water and soil freezing characteristic curves for lean clay. The proposed framework offers a practical and unified approach to describe the strength of variably saturated frozen soils.

papers.title: r- and K-life history strategies drive microbial distribution in distinct soil pore size classes
papers.summary: Life history strategy-based microbial distribution at the soil pore scale was examined using the high-throughput sequencing of bacterial 16S rDNA and fungal ITS region, with functional predictions for bacteria using the bioinformatic tool PICRUSt2. Soil cores (Herndon silt loam with a barley straw) were packed at two bulk densities (1.16 g cm −3 and 0.78 g cm −3 ) to create contrasting pore size distributions. Following saturation, water was selectively removed from specific pore size classes using the pressure plate desorption method at 4, 10, or 100 kPa. Additional treatments for pore water manipulation included unsaturated soil control without water manipulation and wet soil control, i.e., soil subjected to free drainage under open air after saturation. These pore size and moisture manipulations created different pore size classes with varying moistures. Both microbial diversity and community composition were associated with pore size distributions (i.e., bulk density), pore water manipulation, and sampling time. By taking advantage of both soil moisture change and microbial succession during barley straw decomposition, we used the ratio of microbial taxa or predicted functions between day 38 and day 10 of the incubation to infer microbial preferences for specific pore size classes. If microbial distribution had no pore size preference, the ratios for abundance change on day 38 to day 10 should be similar among soils subjected to different pore size and moisture manipulations. The fact that considerable differences occurred among these soil treatments supported microbial pore size preference. Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, often considered as r-strategists/copiotrophs were more abundant in large pores, while Actinobacteria, K-strategists/oligotrophs were relatively enriched in relatively small pores. papers.summary: Abstract. Artificial drainage is widely used in agricultural landscapes to improve trafficability and prevent waterlogging, but comes at the expense of groundwater storage and regional drought resilience. Through model scenarios, this study evaluates how large-scale drain-level adjustments influence groundwater dynamics, water balances, and streamflow extremes across different regions in Flanders, Belgium. A physically based, spatially distributed hydrological model coupling land-surface and groundwater processes was adapted to represent controlled drainage through adjustable weirs, by modifying drain levels and incorporating temporary water storage within drainage ditches behind control structures. Permanently raising drain levels from 1 m to 0.5 m below the surface increased average groundwater levels by 15 cm across Flanders, with increases exceeding 30 cm in actively drained areas. Higher groundwater availability generally resulted in modest increases in evapotranspiration, particularly in flat sandy regions. Simulations showed that raising drain levels shortly after winter (April) was more effective than implementing measures only during summer (June onward), when groundwater tables had often already fallen below the drainage depth. Drainage management also altered streamflow extremes. Under a permanent drain-level increase, low flows increased by 12.8 %. In contrast, summer-only management reduced low flows by up to 10.1 % in some drainage-dominated catchments, highlighting a trade-off between local water retention and downstream water availability. The effects on flood peaks were spatially variable. Peak discharges increased by up to 11.3 % in saturation-prone areas due to reduced unsaturated soil storage, whereas temporary storage behind control structures reduced peak flows by up to 26.5 % in regions dominated by infiltration-excess runoff.
