papers.summary: Abstract The thermal conductivity of unsaturated soils is critical for thermal management in shallow energy infrastructures. Despite growing recognition that soil fabric and drying shrinkage can substantially affect thermal behavior, the underlying physical mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study combines laboratory experiments and numerical simulations to investigate these effects. Experiments were conducted on completely decomposed granite (CDG) and Nanyang clay (NYC), using reconstituted specimens (RS) and compacted specimens (CS) to represent different initial fabric conditions. Results show that RS consistently exhibits higher thermal conductivity than CS at the same saturation and void ratio. Along the drying path, CDG displays a monotonic decrease in thermal conductivity with decreasing saturation, whereas NYC exhibits a nonmonotonic trend, with conductivity increasing at intermediate saturation and peaking at low levels. To interpret these trends, a physics-constrained quartet structure generation set method was developed for pore-scale simulations using experimentally constrained structures and a simplified geometric representation of drying shrinkage. The method captures both the particle-aggregated, dual-porosity structure of CS and the uniform particle arrangement with unimodal pore size distribution found in RS, as well as their distinct fabric evolution induced by drying shrinkage. Simulation results show that RS achieves higher thermal conductivity through well-connected “solid particle chain” pathways, whereas CS depends on more tortuous “solid–liquid bridge–solid” paths caused by aggregates and larger interaggregate pores. The differing thermal conductivity trends in CDG and NYC are further attributed to their distinct shrinkage behaviors, which drive different fabric evolutions and thermal path reconstructions during drying. papers.title: A Particle-Size Fractal Model for Soil Water Characteristic Curve Considering Capillarity and Adsorption
papers.summary: Soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) provide a fundamental description of water retention in unsaturated soils. However, conventional empirical models generally lack an explicit connection between water retention behavior and the multiscale characteristics of soil particle and pore structures. In this study, a full range SWCC model was developed based on particle-size fractal characteristics. The particle-size fractal dimension was used to describe the self-similar characteristics of the particle-size distribution, and a particle-to-pore relationship was established by incorporating the void ratio and the fractal dimension of pore tortuosity. Based on the resulting pore-size distribution, capillary and adsorptive water retention mechanisms were incorporated into a unified fractal framework. The concept of the effective specific thickness of the adsorbed water was introduced to characterize the contribution of particle surface adsorption to water retention at high matric suctions. The proposed model provides a continuous transition from capillary dominated water retention at low suctions to adsorption dominated water retention at high suctions. Its performance was evaluated using six experimental datasets covering clayey soils, silty soils, and sands over a broad range of matric suctions. Compared with the van Genuchten (VG) and Kosugi models, the proposed model achieved the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) for four of the six datasets, while its performance for the other two datasets was broadly comparable to that of the benchmark models. For Arizona silty soil #14, the RMSE was 0.0146, compared with 0.0351 for the VG model and 0.0602 for the Kosugi model, representing reductions of 58.4% and 75.7%, respectively. These comparisons indicate improved fitting performance for several soil types, particularly the silty soils and loess examined in this study. papers.summary: Heavy rainfall can sustain landslide activity for several days after a storm, but daily event inventories often obscure this delayed response and provide little information on the evidence used to infer failure processes. We developed a knowledge-graph workflow that links 2,961 Hong Kong landslide records from 2001 to 2021 with daily rainfall, slope attributes, spatial relations, and 57 investigation reports. Lag analysis was possible for 2,950 records, mechanism analysis for 2,940 records, and 43 events had traceable report anchors. Daily incidence rates and threshold–window tests identified a high-hazard stage on days 0–3 and an extended-hazard stage on days 4–7. With a 50 mm threshold and a 7 days look-back window, 42.2% of events occurred on a qualifying rainfall day and 30.1% occurred during the following week. A nearest-station test using 21 gauges produced 89.4% agreement with the baseline stage classification. The graph combined storm, slope-form, neighborhood, and regional evidence to estimate five mechanism classes. Pore-pressure-dominated soil slides and channelized debris flows accounted for 78.9%–84.4% of classifications across lag stages, while posterior uncertainty increased with lag. Leakage-controlled leave-one-out testing yielded Top-1 and Top-2 accuracies of 0.163 and 0.349. These results support storm-cluster interpretation and investigation prioritization, while event-specific causes still require field evidence.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors. papers.summary: Reconciling high-resolution statistical modeling with geomorphologically meaningful management units remains a challenge in landslide susceptibility assessment. Focusing on the landslide-prone Three Gorges Reservoir area in central China, this study evaluates a framework with three components: (i) a systematic evaluation of statistical metrics (mean, median, standard deviation, range, and IQR for continuous features; mode for categorical features) for feature upscaling within slope units; (ii) a comparative analysis between direct slope-unit modeling (Pixel Feature-to-Slope Unit, PFSU) and a strategy mapping pixel-level predictions to slope units (Pixel Result-to-Slope Unit, PRSU); and (iii) the integration of active deformation monitoring using 166 scenes of Sentinel-1A SBAS-InSAR data (2019–2025). PRSU-Q75-Stacking, combining Stacking with the 75th percentile (Q75) aggregation method, had the highest reported slope-unit AUC in the original evaluation. Coupling the selected susceptibility baseline with InSAR-derived deformation indicators produced a deformation-informed classification that may help prioritize field investigation and monitoring.

Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

Multiobjective Optimization of Landslide Rheological Parameters Based on Random Forest and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II
papers.summary: Abstract Rheological parameters (e.g., pore pressure coefficient r u and dynamic friction angle ϕ ) are necessary input for landslide runout evaluation. However, due to high randomness of initiation, propagation, and accumulation, it is impossible to directly measure rheological properties. This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

Recurrent Landslide Hazards in Ramban District, NW Himalaya, India: An Interplay of Geology, Climate Change, and Anthropogenic Factors
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

Fuzzy logic and frequency ratio based landslide susceptibility mapping using geo environmental and hydro meteorological factors in pithoragarh, uttarakhand
papers.summary: Mass movement events leads to severe infrastructural and socioeconomic damage across the Himalayan belt, particularly in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, India, where over nearly 1,000 events have been recorded in the last two decades. Modelling landslide susceptibility in such highly several, monsoon dominated terrains requires frameworks capable of handling significant spatial and lithological uncertainty. This study assesses and map out regional landslide vulnerability using a Multi Criteria Decision Analysis methodology based on fuzzy logic and frequency ratio. A spatial database comprising fourteen geo spatial and hydro meteorological conditioning factors was integrated to capture the region’s complex topographical and climatic changes. The analytical performances of the models were mathematically validated against a historical landslide inventory using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve. For this uncertain terrain, the Fuzzy Logic model produced a realistic and reliable susceptibility standard with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.686, in the other hand the frequency ratio model provides an AUC of 0.876. In this region, the middle and southern part, which are dominated by unconsolidated soils and heavy monsoon precipitation, are major hazard zones, while the northern side crystalline rock formations are still mostly stable, according to the spatial distribution analysis. So, this verified that the Frequency ratio hazard zonation map offers a data driven, optimal decision support tool compared to fuzzy logic for infrastructure development and disaster risk assessment.

papers.source: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Scientific Mapping and Scientometric Evaluation of Geospatial Technologies in Landslide Research: Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Research Directions
papers.summary: Landslides remain one of the most frequent and destructive natural hazards globally, significantly influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, deforestation, and unplanned developmental activities. In response, geospatial technologies such as Remote Sensing (RS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and machine learning techniques have increasingly been applied to improve landslide prediction, monitoring, susceptibility mapping, and disaster risk reduction. This study presents a bibliometric evaluation of global research trends related to geospatial technologies in landslide studies during the period 2000–2025. A total of 14,909 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus were analysed using the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis identified 2,385 publication sources and an annual scientific growth rate of 14.64%, indicating the rapid expansion of research activities in the field. The study examined publication trends, citation impact, thematic evolution, keyword structure, and international collaboration patterns. The results revealed substantial growth in scientific production, particularly after 2018, driven by advances in spatial data acquisition, artificial intelligence integration, and increasing global disaster risk awareness. China, Italy, India, and the United States emerged as the leading contributors to the research domain. Keyword and thematic analyses demonstrated a clear transition from conventional geomorphological and mapping-based approaches toward advanced machine learning-driven predictive modelling and geospatial monitoring frameworks. The study further identified two major interconnected research streams: remote sensing-based monitoring and GIS-based susceptibility modelling. Improved Landslide Detection in Southeastern Xizang Based on L-DCGAN-Augmented Data and the L-YOLOv8 Model
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are common geological disasters that cause extensive damage and significant harm. Efficient recognition of landslide remote sensing images holds both theoretical and practical importance. However, practical landslide detection faces challenges including limited data, high computation, large memory use, and low accuracy. In this study, high-quality landslide remote sensing images were collected from southeastern Xizang to construct a landslide remote sensing data set. To address the issue of insufficient samples, an improved model, landslide-deep convolutional generative adversarial network (L-DCGAN), based on DCGAN, was proposed to enhance landslide remote sensing data. The enhanced data set was constructed by incorporating efficient channel attention (ECA) and squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules into the generator and discriminator, respectively. Additionally, an improved YOLOv8 model, landslide-you only look once version 8(L-YOLOv8), was proposed. First, the cross-stage partial pyramid convolution (CSPPC) and grouped and shuffled convolution (GSConv) modules replaced the cross stage partial layer with 2 branches (C2f) module and ordinary convolution in the network to reduce the number of model parameters and computational complexity. Then, the spatial and channel synergistic attention (SCSA) mechanism was introduced to improve detection accuracy. Experimental results showed that compared with the original YOLOv8 algorithm, the number of model parameters in L-YOLOv8 was reduced by approximately 41.78%, and the average accuracy on the landslide sample data set was increased by 0.57%, and frames per second (FPS) was improved by 33.87%. The model achieved lightweight design while improving detection speed and accuracy, and demonstrated superior performance on the landslide remote sensing data set.

Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.source: Journal of Structural Design and Construction Practice
papers.summary: Abstract A reconnaissance mission was organized by the American Concrete Institute, Committee 133, to visit the Los Grillos Bridge in Colombia on September 13, 2023. The bridge is a post-tensioned cast-in-place segmental cantilever structure featuring a box girder spanning 180 m. Situated on a slow-moving landslide, the bridge failed on August 20, 2023. Analyses indicated that the concrete crushing of the bottom slab of the 180-m-long box girder triggered the failure. This case study demonstrates that similar structures can withstand large relative deformations in the transverse direction and differential settlements, yet they remain quite vulnerable to displacement in the longitudinal direction. It also highlights the susceptibility of bridge structures in unstable geological regions.

Impact of Rainfall Infiltration on Groundwater Seepage under the Effect of Urban Construction in Shanghai
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

Closed-Form Solutions for Temperature-Dependent Suction Stress under Transient Infiltration in Unsaturated Soil: An Application for Stability Analysis of Strip Plate Anchors
papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

Vertical Acceleration Effect on Slope Stability: A Simplified Coupled Insight
papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

A cost-benefit analysis of mine slope stability with consideration of risk losses
papers.summary: Purpose This study aims to develop a probabilistic cost-benefit analysis framework for mine slope reinforcement, addressing the growing challenges of slope instability in coal mining areas. The model evaluates the impact of reinforcement measures on the probability of slope failure and economic performance, providing a decision-making tool for selecting cost-effective stabilization strategies. Design/methodology/approach A two-dimensional slope model was constructed using the Limit Equilibrium Method, incorporating failure probabilities derived under varying geological and mechanical assumptions. The framework integrates slope stability analysis, uncertainty modeling, and cost estimation, including initial investment, reinforcement expenses, risk-related losses, and post-failure restoration costs. A case study from the Jianbei Coal Mine in Shaanxi Province, China, was used to compare multiple reinforcement schemes combining different numbers and lengths of upper and lower anchors, with and without slope cutting. Findings The results indicate that anchoring reinforcement generally exhibits superior cost-effectiveness compared to slope cutting in the studied case. However, an optimal reinforcement level is identified, beyond which additional anchoring leads to diminishing returns and unnecessary cost escalation without corresponding safety benefits. The model captures the interaction between geological uncertainty, reinforcement design, and economic performance. Originality/value This study presents a novel probabilistic cost-benefit analysis method that explicitly incorporates slope failure probability into reinforcement decision-making. The proposed model provides a practical tool for evaluating reinforcement strategies under uncertainty, supporting optimized and economically efficient slope stabilization in mining engineering.

Rapid Assessment of Seismic Slope Stability Considering the Increase of Excess Pore-Water Pressure
papers.summary: Abstract For soil slopes, excess pore-water pressure (EPWP) buildup in soil elements is a major cause of slope failure during seismic loading. In this study, an EPWP coefficient was proposed and integrated into the simplified Bishop method to rapidly assess the influence of EPWP buildup on seismic slope stability and to calculate the slope factor of safety. To determine the value of the EPWP coefficient, numerical simulations of soil slopes with different inclinations were performed. During seismic loading, the decrease in the factor of safety for the slope can be clearly observed with the increase in EPWP. It was found that the value of the EPWP coefficient was negatively correlated with the slope angle. A linear function was employed to fit the correlation between the EPWP coefficient and the slope angle. It enables easy prediction of the EPWP coefficient based on the slope geometry and further facilitates seismic slope stability analysis that considers the EPWP buildup.

Landslide Dams Triggered by Extreme Rainfall Events: A Tairāwhiti Gisborne Case Study
papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. Two large landslide dams were chosen as case studies, the 1,485,500 m3 Waiorongomai Landslide Dam which formed in the north of the region in early January 2023, and the 98,500 m3 Tiniroto Landslide Dam which formed in the south of the region on the 3rd of October 2023. Three elements of analyses were used to investigate these landslide dams. First, historic landslides were mapped in the two catchments, to investigate the rate of landslide-river connectivity and landslide dam frequency. Each landslide source and deposit were mapped as polygons, using aerial imagery between 1988 and 2023. Second, the short-term evolution of the Waiorongomai and Tiniroto landslide dams was documented through a series of engineering geomorphic maps, using LiDAR and aerial imagery in ArcGIS Pro. Finally, the grain size distribution, liquid and plastic limits, and slake durability were analysed

papers.title: Developing Mitigation Measures against Rainfall-induced Shallow Landslides using Plant Root Systems
Landslide susceptibility mapping using a physically-based model: the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna meteorological event
papers.source: AMS Laurea Institutional Research Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are an increasingly frequent hazard, with a direct impact on the land and on the people who live on it. Physically-based models assess their susceptibility by coupling a mechanical stability analysis with a hydrological description of the slope. The difficulty lies in the choice of the input parameters. The geotechnical and hydrological properties these models require cannot be measured at catchment scale: they have to be assumed within plausible intervals and calibrated on the observed landslides. Two major rainfall events struck the Emilia-Romagna region of Italy in May 2023. They triggered thousands of shallow landslides in the Apennine sector, mostly debris slides and debris flows, on slopes where no instability had been recorded before. This thesis applies the Fast Shallow Landslide Assessment Model (FSLAM) to the municipal territory of Casola Valsenio (84 km², 100 to 960 m a.s.l.), calibrating and evaluating it on the inventory compiled immediately afterwards. The purpose is not the best performance the model can give, but a measure of what each modelling choice is worth. Six configurations were compared on a common basis, fixed in advance: the validation dataset, the search space of the parameters and the selection rule. They differ in the calibration strategy and in the structure of the model. Across the six, accuracy ranges from 0.653 to 0.665 and the area under the ROC curve from 0.703 to 0.740, while the parameter sets that produce them differ by orders of magnitude. What the choices do change is the operating point of the model, the plausibility of the calibrated parameters and the consistency of the state of the slopes before the event. Accuracy alone therefore cannot select the parameters. Physical plausibility has to be set as a criterion before the calibration, not read off the results afterwards. What limits the model here is not its formulation, but the spatial information it can draw on.

papers.source: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
papers.summary: Regional Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) are essential tools for predicting rainfall-induced slope instability across broad geographic regions. This thesis provides an evaluation of the regional LEWS in Catalonia, Spain, assessing its real-time operational performance and sensitivity across operational factors (2024–2025) and its forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h predictive lead times (2024–2026). The system inputs include precipitation datasets, Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) and Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF), alongside a regional static susceptibility map and an official reported landslide inventory The evaluation framework applies an adapted Event-Duration Matrix (EDuMaP) methodology combined with spatial-fuzzy verification across slope units, municipalities, and counties. Real-time evaluations against reported landslide inventories showed that applying quality-control data filtering and a 48 h fuzzy verification window significantly improved system Hit Rates, confirming that inventory timing uncertainties often mask successful alerts. Factor sensitivity and multi-factor clustering revealed that during that while the real-time forecasting the system captures medium-to-large shallow slides and debris flows during intense convective storms (𝐼𝑒𝑞 higher than 50 mm/h, detecting 80–85% of events), structural blind spots exist. Current operational triggers miss slope failures driven by low-to-moderate rainfall (𝐼𝑒𝑞 lower than 30 mm/h) due to fixed 24 h accumulation windows that ignore antecedent rainfall and soil moisture, fine-scale road-cut failures smoothed out by 30 m DEM resolution, and lowsusceptibility mapped zones. Evaluating forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h lead times revealed that performance drops substantially as lead times extend, with 𝐻𝑅𝑊 decreasing to ~25% and 𝑃𝑃𝑊falling to 36.0–50.0% at 48 h. This degradation is driven by atmospheric forecast error accumulation and the shift from hybrid observed-forecast i

papers.title: Development of an AI-Driven Model to Predict Slope Collapse Due to Rainfall
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.title: Base-level lowering rates control a landslide process transition in California's Franciscan mélange
papers.summary: California’s Franciscan mélange is well-known for hosting persistent, slow-moving earthflows, a landslide style favored by the unit’s significant local variability in shear strength (e.g. Medley, 2001; Kim et al., 2004; Roering et al., 2015). Big Sur’s mélange, however, is unusual: landslide mapping there reveals both recent (e.g. the 2017 Mud Creek landslide) and prehistoric rotational landslides on slopes that are unusually steep for this lithology. Because rotational landslides and earthflows pose markedly different hazards, understanding what drives the shift in failure style is critical for hazard assessment. Here we test the hypothesis that the rate of base-level lowering governs the transition between earthflow and rotational failure. We synthesize landslide mapping and analysis of high-resolution topography across two Franciscan mélange settings with contrasting rates of base-level lowering: the South Fork Eel River canyon, where river incision drives base-level lowering at ~1 mm/yr, and the southern Big Sur coast, where wave erosion drives local base-level lowering at ~2 cm/yr. We then use 2-D numerical modeling to test whether rapid coastal retreat alone can drive a transition from earthflow to rotational failure in a Franciscan mélange hillslope.Landslide mapping shows that landslide activity in Big Sur, as defined by InSAR-derived deformation rates, is concentrated along the actively eroding coastline, and that the two regions differ systematically in failure style according to overall hillslope angle. Big Sur’s steeper slopes are dominated by rotational landslides, while the Eel River region’s shallower slopes are dominated by earthflows. Numerical modeling shows that progressive lateral erosion can produce rotational failure on hillslopes that were previously deforming as earthflows, provided there is some degree of vertical heterogeneity in the weathering profile. Taken together, these results indicate that changes in the rate of base-level lowering c

papers.title: Digital soil mapping of mountain soils: from pedodiversity to land vocation and ecosystem services
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: This doctoral research explored the application of Geographic Information System (GIS) and Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) techniques to improve soil mapping processes and support land management and biodiversity conservation, in alignment with the objectives of the National Biodiversity Future Center (NBFC). The study was conducted in two Regional Parks of the Northern Apennines, a region characterized by high environmental heterogeneity and a rich cartographic heritage. Traditional pedological knowledge and expert-driven selection of environmental covariates were first employed to delineate land units and produce a conventional soil map. Subsequently, DSM approaches using Random Forest models with recursive feature elimination were applied to generate an alternative soil map based on DEM derivatives and remotely sensed data, achieving high accuracy and interpretability. The analysis identified key drivers of soil differentiation, such as topography, insolation, vegetation indices, and proximity to water bodies, highlighting their potential for transferability to similar areas and for overcoming cartographic discontinuities. Complementary studies on the same area revealed that climate exerts a stronger influence than vegetation on soil evolution, and that considering soil diversity enhances understanding of organic matter dynamics. The second component of this research addressed the reestablishment of chestnut cultivation in the Northern Apennines through a land suitability model that was tested on the municipality of Castel del Rio (BO). The resulting map identified both underutilized suitable lands and cultivated areas with significant limitations, findings that were corroborated by the severe landslides of May 2023. Moreover, the study suggested that land morphology and soil characteristics may influence the spread of ink disease, a major threat to chestnut groves. Overall, this research demonstrates the value of integrating GIS-based modeling, soil science, and ecol

papers.title: Analisis Kerawanan Longsorlahan di Kabupaten Wonogiri Berdasarkan Sistem Informasi Geografis
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
authors: , Dr. Annisa Trisnia Sasmi, S.Si., M.T
papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.title: INTEGRASI PERSISTENT SCATTERER INTERFEROMETRIC SYNTHETIC APERTURE RADAR (PS-INSAR) DAN ANALYTICAL HIERARCHY PROCESS (AHP) UNTUK PEMETAAN KERAWANAN LONGSOR DI SEKITAR LAPANGAN PANAS BUMI WAYANG WINDU
papers.source: Repository at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia (Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia)
papers.summary: Kawasan Panas Bumi Wayang Windu merupakan wilayah yang memiliki potensi tanah longsor yang tinggi. Pemetaan kerawanan longsor umumnya masih menggunakan parameter statis sehingga belum sepenuhnya merepresentasikan kondisi pergerakan permukaan tanah secara aktual. Oleh karena itu, penelitian ini bertujuan mengintegrasikan informasi deformasi permukaan hasil PS-InSAR ke dalam metode Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) untuk pemetaan kerawanan longsor serta mengevaluasi tingkat akurasi hasil pemetaan di sekitar Lapangan Panas Bumi Wayang Windu. Penelitian memanfaatkan 60 citra Sentinel-1A periode 2024–2026, serta beberapa parameter kerawanan longsor lainnya seperti kemiringan lereng, curah hujan, penggunaan lahan, jenis tanah, jenis batuan, dan jarak dari patahan. Pembobotan parameter dilakukan menggunakan AHP berdasarkan penilaian ahli, kemudian seluruh parameter diintegrasikan melalui analisis weighted overlay. Hasil pengolahan PS-InSAR menunjukkan deformasi Line of Sight (LOS) berkisar antara -33 hingga 38 mm/tahun yang menunjukkan adanya fenomena subsidence dan uplift. Integrasi deformasi permukaan ke dalam model AHP menghasilkan peta kerawanan longsor empat kelas, yaitu rendah, sedang, tinggi, dan sangat tinggi. Hasil validasi menggunakan matriks konfusi menunjukkan nilai Overall Accuracy sebesar 95,4% dan koefisien Kappa sebesar 93,4%, yang menunjukkan bahwa integrasi PS-InSAR dan AHP mampu menghasilkan pemetaan kerawanan longsor dengan tingkat ketelitian yang baik serta dapat mendukung upaya mitigasi bencana di sekitar Panas Bumi Wayang Windu. The Wayang Windu Geothermal Field is an area with a high potential for landslides. Landslide susceptibility mapping generally relies on static parameters, which do not fully represent actual ground surface movement. Therefore, this study aims to integrate surface deformation information derived from PS-InSAR into the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) for landslide susceptibility mapping and to evaluate the accuracy of the r

papers.title: Advances in the detection and monitoring of mass-movement processes through high-resolution remote sensing data
papers.summary: With advances in satellite technology, spaceborne data are becoming available to the public and scientific community at increasing temporal and spatial resolutions. These data open new opportunities to study Earth-surface processes in unprecedented detail. This thesis investigates the potential and challenges of high-resolution optical data for monitoring slow-moving landslides and the generation of digital elevation models (DEMs) to improve subsequent topographic analyses. The study area is set in the northwest Argentinean Andes -- a region particularly susceptible to mass movement processes due to steep topography, heavy rainfall during the summer monsoon, and geologic pre-conditioning. To obtain a more detailed reconstruction of local topography, tri-stereo SPOT-7 data were used to infer a 3-m DEM of the intermontane Quebrada del Toro basin through stereophotogrammetry. GNSS field measurements were employed to validate the derived elevations and identify optimal processing parameters. In steep mountain terrain, where global radar-derived DEMs frequently suffer from layover and shadowing effects, high-resolution stereo data can help to reduce artifacts and better resolve the traces of channelized processes. The longitudinal channel profiles extracted from the 3-m DEM contain topographic signatures of both fluvial erosion and debris flows, which are based on the relationship between slope and drainage area. Debris-flow activity is presumed to dominate in channels that exhibit minimal curvature despite an increase in drainage areas. The topographic signature of debris-flow activity is found throughout the Toro basin, fueled by pervasively fractured bedrock along the major bounding fault systems. Mass-movement processes are also common in the neighboring Quebrada de Humahuaca basin. papers.title: Assessing the influence of rainfall-induced desiccation cracking on slope stability in Malaysia
papers.summary: The influence of climate change on slope stability has become increasingly relevant in recent years, particularly in tropical regions like Malaysia, where the frequency and severity of rainfall events are anticipated to vary considerably. This study examined the combined impacts of rainfall variability and soil desiccation cracking on the slope stability in Malaysia’s tropical granitic residual soils. The study conducted a comprehensive analysis of precipitation patterns utilizing both historical and projected climatic data across multiple climate change scenarios. It subsequently investigated the formation of desiccation cracks in soils exposed to repeated cycles of wetting and drying under controlled laboratory circumstances, replicating actual seasonal variations. Numerical models evaluated the impact of rainfall infiltration on slope stability amid changing climatic circumstances. The rainfall pattern analysis revealed a notable tendency of increasing wet-season rainfall but a considerable decline in dry-season precipitation. This extreme climate condition has provoked the formation of desiccation cracks on soil slopes. The subsequent experimental study indicated that desiccation cracks substantially enhance water infiltration into the soil. The mechanism involved increased crack formation with the repetitive wetting-drying cycles, leading to increased void ratio in soil, and hence resulted in a higher permeability. The numerical analysis reported that slopes with gentler gradients exhibited less sensitivity to climate change impact, with average Factor of Safety (FOS) values of about 0.8, 0.95, and 1.1 for slopes of 1V:1H, 1V:1.5H, and 1V:2H, respectively, under future rainfall conditions. From 2024 to 2070, the percentage of time during which FOS fell below 1.0 was 91.4%, 70.1%, and 35.3% for these three slope gradients under the MIROC5_RCP8.5 scenario (and 90.5%, 67.4%, and 27.3% under MIROC5_RCP4.5), indicating a substantial reduction in stability. papers.title: Multi-hazard modelling of hydro-geomorphological events for early warning systems. Application to the Val d’Aran (Central Pyrenees, Spain)
papers.summary: (English) Hydro-geomorphological hazards such as floods and rainfall-induced landslides frequently co-occur in mountainous regions, driven by shared meteorological forcing but governed by distinct hydrological and geotechnical mechanisms. Improving their anticipation requires modelling frameworks capable of consistently representing subsurface hydrological conditioning and its interaction with transient triggering processes. This thesis develops and evaluates a physically based, forecast-driven multi-hazard modelling framework for early warning applications in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Val d’Aran, Central Pyrenees, Spain). The research progresses through three interconnected stages. First, an event-based slope stability model is enhanced through a novel multi-objective calibration strategy that explicitly represents both antecedent and final slope stability conditions. Results demonstrate that inadequate representation of subsurface hydrological states leads to physically inconsistent pre-event instability, highlighting the sensitivity of slope response to antecedent moisture conditions. Building on this finding, a continuous distributed hydrological–geotechnical modelling system (SCLAM) is developed to dynamically simulate snowmelt, rainfall–runoff processes, groundwater redistribution, and slope stability within a unified framework. By replacing externally imposed antecedent conditions with internally simulated hydrological states, the model improves physical consistency and identifies Baseflow Excess as a main indicator of destabilizing subsurface conditions. The coupled framework is subsequently extended into a prototype multi-hazard early warning system integrating flood and landslide forecasting under bias-corrected ensemble meteorological forcings. papers.title: Engineering geological properties of the Awhitu Group sands at Muriwai, New Zealand
papers.summary: Landslides are a critical risk to New Zealand’s infrastructure and economy, as evidenced during the widespread early 2023 storms. The Awhitu Group sands are late Pliocene to early Pleistocene dune sands and associated facies found throughout the New Zealand North Island west coast. Muriwai, a settlement in the Auckland region, has an 80 m escarpment consisting of Awhitu Group sands that failed as fatal landslides during strong rainfall in early 2023 and in 1965. Interestingly, there is currently limited research on the geotechnical properties of the Awhitu Group sands, particularly at Muriwai. Therefore, this study aims to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the engineering geology properties of the Muriwai Awhitu Group sands to gain more appreciation for the complexity of this geological unit and the Muriwai slope conditions. Awhitu Group sands at or near the 2023 Muriwai landslide areas were sampled and tested in-situ with a shear vane and handheld penetrometer. Subsequently, laboratory work was conducted on the Muriwai Awhitu Group sand samples such as particle size analysis, Atterberg limits and linear shrinkage tests, dispersion experiments, X-Ray Fluorescence analysis, Scanning Electron Microscope and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy investigations, as well direct shear tests. Additionally, digital ArcGIS examinations were undertaken to assess the dimensions and pre-failure topography of the 2023 Muriwai landslide areas. The Muriwai Awhitu Group sand samples were found to be predominantly poorly graded very fine to medium sands that have some low plasticity active clays. The samples were mostly composed of quartz, aluminosilicates (including feldspars, smectite, halloysite, allophane, kaolinite and illite), and some iron. Moreover, the samples were generally non-expansive, non-dispersive, moderately sensitive, stiff to hard, and moderately cemented with some high cohesion and internal friction angle values.
